TREATY WITH UNITED STATES RE BOUNDARY AND FISHERIES.
speechtext:
I would call the attention of the right hon. the First Minister to the following paragraph which appears in this morning's ' Citizen ' :
Washington, April 11.-Secretary of State Root and British Ambassador Bryce to-day signed two treaties negotiated recently between the United States and Great Britain One provides for a commission to determine the boundary between the United States and Canada and the other regulates fishing in the great lakes and contiguous streams. The boundary commission will be charged with the work of resurveying certain sections of boundary line and determining disputed questions in that connection. It is said that the fishery question also is placed in the hands of a commission by the terms of the treaty.
Are the government in a position to give the House information ? Have they any control over the appointment of the commissioners or over their selection, especially on behalf of Canada?
Rt. Hon. Sir WILFRID LAUR1ER (Prime Minister). 1 have just received a telegram stating that these two treaties have been signed. One refers to the boundary. It is not contemplated to establish new boundaries but simply mark again the boundaries and describe them on maps. The second deals with the fisheries. In the contiguous waters, we have had difficulties for many years owing to there being a close season on our side and none on the American side. By the treaty all contiguous waters will be put under a commission which will make regulations for the fisheries. The appointments on the British side exclusively belong to the government of Canada.

SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to call the attention of the government to the fact that some of their officers in the city of Halifax are taking undue and improper interest in an election to the neglect of the duties for which they are appointed and for which they are being paid by this country. It seems that at the present time there is a civic election going on in Halifax and that Dr. A. C. Hawkins is a candidate for mayor. This Dr. A. C. Hawkins is also the health officer at the port of Halifax, for which he receives a salary of $1,000 a year, together with a couple of very nice uniforms covered with gold lace, an overcoat and two or three hats and caps. He has also called to his assistance iu this civic campaign a number of other officers of the government, notably one E. M. Wilson, foreman of the car cleaners at the North street station, and one Albert Tobin, of the round house staff at Richmond. I would call the attention of the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham! to this fact. There is also one Wm. Merlin, of the Department of Marine and Fisheries.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Merwin ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Not Merwin, but Merlin, the enchanter. There is also one Geo. McNamara, of the Department of Marine and Fisheries. These people are taking a very active interest in the election, and I believe that so intense is the devotion of Dr. Hawkins to his camnaign that a ship with a thousand immigrants has been held at quarantine-delayed-because this gentleman is canvassing for the position of mayor of the city of Halifax rather than attending to the duty for which he is paid. I think this is a matter of very great importance, and in view of the declarations that have been made by the various ministers in regard to public officials taking part in elections some severe examples should be made of these gentlemen.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: We should have some explanation from the Minister of Railways,

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: particularly as a similar matter has been brought to his attention two or three times this session already. Surely the minister is going to take some action. Is he going to treat with contempt the circular which was issued by Mr. Fottinger and which said that employees of the Intercolonial Railway should not as a general thing run for municipal office.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: That is different.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: In what respect?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: There is no suggestion in this case that an Intercolonial Railway official is running for office.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I understand that some of these are Intercolonial Railway employees.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: No. It is merely stated that he is calling to his aid some men to help him. These men are citizens and I suppose they have the right to vote.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: They are employees of the Intercolonial Railway who are doing partisan work in connection with municipal affairs .

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: What is there partisan about it?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: There is this : An employee of the Intercolonial Railway goes into the shops and threatens the men if they do not vote so and so. That is partisan work.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: That never was suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: No, no.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: In my opinion he has a letter in his hand which specifies that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: He may, but he did not say so.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
Is this quarantine doctor to be allowed to employ his time, for which he is paid by the country, in canvassing for the position of mayor and leave a vessel detained outside the harbour with
1.000	immigrants and no one to attend to them. Has the Prime Minister nothing ttf say about that ? The Minister of Railways laughs as though it were an amusing thing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: It is, very.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: What is there amusing about it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: The amusement is that my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is lecturing me while he is discussing the acts of an official who does not belong to my department at all.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I was speaking about employees of the Intercolonial.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: They are not candidates.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: They are canvassers, and partisan canvassers at that, and they are deliberately violating the rule laid down by the Prime Minister a few years ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Is this doctor a Grit or a Tory.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I never inquired, and I don't know anything about his politics. Recently I was told when I called attention to a similar case with regard to employees on the Intercolonial that I was pitching into a Tory. I don't care a straw about that, because if it is wrong in a Grit it is wrong in a Tory, and I have no standard by which I draw a distinction between the two in tiiese matters. No matter what party an official belongs to I say it is wrong.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
I understand the Minister of Railways to say that no charge has been made against officials of the Intercolonial taking part in elections, but I have a letter with regard to the same matter. Let me read this passage from the ' Gazette ' :
Not only did this terrible delay mean that the passengers were kept in confinement and without food for a. day, but everything at the immigration station during the doctor's absence was at a standstill. Four trains were delayed for six hours, and all the other immigration officials and the railway men were kept idle.
I think that should be looked luto.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: That does not at all refer to any member of the Intercolonial staff being a candidate or being absent from liis employment.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: It is the medical officer.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: It does not follow at all from the statements read by the hon. member that any employee of the Intercolonial Railway is a candidate in an election. Now, as to the general question and so far as the employees of the Intercolonial Railway are concerned, I may say that this matter is probably more strictly considered on that railway than on any other railway in Canada. In my own town the employees of the Grand Trunk are not only candidates themselves but they take an active part in municipal elections. Are you going to say to a brakesman or to any other employee of a railway: You are to be disfranchised, you must not say a word to your neighbour about municipal politics; you must not take any interest whatever in municipal affairs. Well, I believe the peo-p'e of Canada do not want that kind of thing.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: The Grank Trunk is not a government railway.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: This is a thing that has to be considered from the point of view of common ordinary horse sense. I say that an employee of the Intercolonial Railway should not be offensive, and it is better he should not be a municipal candidate unless-there is some exceptional consideration, but to say that he must not take any part in the municipal government for which he is taxed is going to the length of absurdity, even if the railway is owned by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: There is only one point in the observations of bon. gentlemen opposite which really deserves consideration, and that is that a steamship with a large number of immigrants has been detained unduly by reason of the neglect of the medical officer. That is a matter which certainly well deserves consideration. But lion, gentlemen will see that the mere publication of a statement in a newspaper, and a newspaper which is noc supposed to be entirely beyond the suspicion of political bias, is hardly sufficient ground for the government to take action against the officer. If any hon. gentleman who has knowledge himself will send a statement to the proper minister that any officer of his department has neglected his business in the manner described, that would be a proper matter for investigation. Now as to the partisan side of it. My bon. friend (Mr. Sproule) says be does not know whether this candidate is a Grit or a Tory. I accept his statement, but if he does not know whether the man is a Grit or a Tory how does be bring the partisan element into the question at all ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: The partisan element is that he threatened employees they would be dismissed if they did not do so and so.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
We have bad no such statement made to tbe House. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule! lias imported that into the discussion. The hon. gentleman from King's and Albert did not make that statement, and it would appear that the bon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) is giving away more of tbe game than was intended. However that may be, the only point worthy of consideration is as to whether this officer in Halifax has neglected his duty. There is a distinction between a municipal and a Dominion or provincial election. We were asked earlier in the session to lay down some rule with regard to municipal elections elsewhere, and it is a very difficult matter to do so. A rule may be laid down with respect to a Dominion election and probably with respect to a provincial election also, but it may be a question as to whether you would be justified, iu the case of a man who happens to be a citizen of a municipality and a Dominion official at the same time, in refusing him the right to take part in a municipal elec-

tion. But if in doing so he should neglect his public duties, then unquestionably that would be a proper matter for investigation, and I am sure that the minister in whose department such an officer is employed would feel it his duty to investgate any representations to that effect which might be properly made. _

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to the remarks of the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) and the replies of gentlemen on this side of the House, I wish to call attention to the fact that Mr. Hawkins is receiving money from the government. He is medical officer at the port of Halifax under the Interior Department. I shall read an article in the Ottawa ' Journal ' of to-day, which gives a full description of the occurrences at Halifax. The article is as follows :
Halifax, Nova Scotia, April 13.-The immigration department at Halifax have furnished another subject for government investigation. Formal complaint has been made to the Ottawa government of what amounts to inhuman treatment of a large number of the 1,100 passengers who came by the Allan steamer
lunisian ' from Liverpool.
Ihe official who is charged in this complaint ls.-Dr* A. C. Hawkins, the chief medical officer, without whose certificate no passenger can leave the detention room at the immigration sheds. The passengers had breakfast on board the steamer, and many of them were kept without food till 11.30 that night, when the last of the crowd was passed.
Dr. Hawkins began his examination at 3 o clock in the afternoon, the people then tired out with the long waiting. He worked for three hours and stopped at six, then leaving the building not to return till 9.45 p.m., when the task was resumed on an almost famished assemblage of angry people. He got through shortly before midnight.
Not only did this terrible delay mean that the passengers were kept in confinement and without food for a day, but everything at the immigration station during the doctors absence was at a standstill. Four trains were delayed for six hours, and all the other immigration onicials and the railway men were kept idle. The half-starving passengers, as well as those who had got through and were waiting to get off, naturally made a great outcry and vowed vengeance.
The doctor is conducting an active election canvass, which may account for his absence, but this did not mitigate the condition of the nunareas of passengers, who were practical prisoners without food.
Under tlie circumstances I feel that members^ on this side of the House are thoroughly justified in bringing forward this question and demanding from the Minister of the Interior some explanation in regard to it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:

Mr. FIELDING
the minister should take formal notice of it. Mi-. ARMSTRONG. I was addressing the Minister of the Interior. I cannot understand how the hon. gentleman comes in.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
Through you, Mr. Sneaker, I addressed my hon. friend, and I was pointing out to him, through you, the very absurd position he occupies before the House and before you. If a charge is brought against this officer of the Department of the Interior I have no doubt the Minister of the Interior will look carefully into the matter. I am sure every hon. member on this side of the House will agree that this course should be taken.
However, we have here a question of much greater importance than the question of whether a certain official in Halifax is a candidate for tlie municipal elections. On the general question of the relation of government officials to municipal politics I hold the view that acceptance of office by any citizen of this country should not debar him from participating in municipal matters in the community in which lie lives.
I hope every member on this side will take the same view, and I wish the position taken by the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) to-day to be distinctly understood not only in this House, but in the country at large. Hon. gentlemen opposite have laid down a position which I am sure when It is understood by tlie people of Canada will not meet with their approval. It is that if a man accepts office at tlie hands of,the Dominion government, no matter how small or how great that office may be, from that time forward he is to take no part whatever in municipal matters in the town or city in which he resides. It means that government employees abandon all claims of citizenship where they reside. That is the position taken by the hon. member for

Grey (Mr. Sproule), who is leading the opposition at the moment, and who speaks as the leader of his party and lays down the policy of his party in this matter. It is to the effect that henceforth men occupying positions on any part of the Intercolonial Railway must not take any part in municipal matters. It is well for the people of the country generally to realize the position taken by these hon. gentlemen. I hold, as I have always held, the view expressed by the Minister of Railways this afternoon, that men employed on the Intercolonial Railway have a perfect right to assert themselves in municipal matters in the towns or villages in which they reside. I shall do all in my power to maintain that right for them. They are residents of the municipality ; they pay taxes, and why should they not participate in civic matters? Why should they not with me have the right to determine who is and who is not a fit person to represent them on a municipal board? Our lion, friends opposite will deny that right. We on this side are content to have our policy on this matter go to the country side by side with that of our friends opposite, who assert this afternoon that henceforth their policy is to be to deprive these men of all rights as citizens.
lion. II. R. EMMERSON (Westmoreland). I do not wish to prolong this debate, but I entirely endorse every word uttered by the hon. member for Sydney (Mr. Johnston). If the government undertake to control the officials of the Interior Department or any government official with respect to the exercise of their civic rights, they might just as well undertake to say what fraternal societies their officials should join and what churches they should attend. It seems to me that the doctrine laid down by the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Sproule) is entirely too absurd and will not be accepted by the citizenship of this country in any province.

speechtext:
I wish to draw the attention of the Minister of Railways, to a despatch which appeared in the Winnipeg ' Telegram ' dated April 1st, 1008:
Fearful death record in work on National Railway.
In a period of one year from March 29, 1907, to March 31, 1908, the lives of fifty men have been sacrificed through negligence or carelessness on a hundred mile stretch of the National Transcontinental Railway between the Manitoba boundary and the east end of Canyon lake, a distance of a hundred miles. This does not include those who have been killed on the section east of Vermillion, nor does it take note of the scores of poor fellows who have lost eyes or limbs on those sections of the National Transcontinental.
Further the article says :
It is a weekly, often daily, affair to hear of the horrible deaths which men meet with, to say nothing of the hundreds who are brought to the hospital here mangled, maimed and dying, either to linger on through countless hours of agony, or to recover and go through life with the loss of a limb, an eye, or sometimes of both.
Further on the writer adds:
Jury asked for safeguards.
When death's harvest first began, some two years ago. a coroner's jury memorialized the Deoartment of Railways to take some action to safeguard the lives of the workers. How much notice was taken of the memorial may be judged by the fact that the act of that jury had to be repeated bv another, only a fortnight ago, and still Ottawa is silent.
And further on:
Over a man a mile.
It is freely stated in Kenora that on a section of Dutton & McArthur's work, stretching ten miles east of the Winnipeg river, the toll of human life expended was over a man a mile. Perhaps the fifteen miles on the south side of Canyon lake, north of Vermillion, will mark the deathbeds of more men than any other on the hundred mile stretch already alluded to and depicted on the accompanying map.
This newspaper gives the names of forty-eight who have been killed on this line of railway. It would take too long to read the list, but I am quite sure the attention of the minister has been directed to this and other articles referring to the same question. Two causes are given. One is criminal negligence in the use of low grade explosives, and the second is inexperienced workmen. These two points should receive Mr. SAM. nUGHES
special attention from the Minister of Railways. The minister should not permit his contractors to use cheap explosives or he must expect to have a heavy death rate. I am much surprised that after the grand jury had directed attention to this some time ago, it was necessary for another grand jury to make a second reference to it. We cannot afford, as a Canadian people, in the construction of our railways, to have hundreds of lives taken by carelessness, either on the part of the government or the contractors..

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
The question raised is one of considerable seriousness. The construction of the government portion of the Transcontinental is in the hands of a commission. That commission is responsible to the government and to parliament and has absolute control of the details. Accidents have taken place under the contractors ; my hon. friends say there are two causes, namely, carelessness and low grade explosives. I am not in a position to dispute this statement nor do I suppose he is in a position to confirm it. There may be low grade explosives and there may not. That is a statement made by a newspaper. And possibly neither he nor I know if it be true. One thing is certain and that is that the death rate caused by accidents is of sufficient seriousness to attract attention and investigation. It has not escaped my attention altogether. I have had several interviews with the cliairman-of the Transcontinental Commission. It is pointed out to me that men using explosives become so accustomed to their work that they become oblivious of the danger and it is to their own carelessness largely that these accidents are due. That may he partially the case or may not, but my bon. friend will remember that this is one of the difficulties in getting at the truth of these matters. The legal way to locate the blame is through a coroner's inquest. The holding of an inquest is supposed to be the modus operand! by which the Crown or the public will get at the cause of the accident and will ascertain whether there has been criminal negligence in the case. A few years ago, the Ontario legislature, not being satisfied with the results of coroners' investigations in cases of accident in the construction of great works, passed an amendment to the Act making it more stringent. One of the clauses provided, if I remember correctly-and I am speaking from memory,-that no coroner could hold an investigation who was the medical attendant upon the men for the railway companies, and that no coroner could take part in such an investigation who had an interest directly or indirectly in a contract with the company. There were other provisions, if I remember well, by which the Attorney General took special steps to see that the

investigation was carried on properly. I have asked this question recently of the chairman of the commission and expect to have an answer in a few days as to some of the particulars, if the spirit as well as the letter of the provincial law was being carried out in the holding of these inquests. If it be, there will be no difficulty in arriving at a conclusion as to the direct cause of these accidents. If carelessness on the part of the workmen be the cause the coroner and the representative of the Attorney General should be able to ascertain the facts. If the contractors are using low-grade explosives, there should be no difficulty in the coroner arriving at that fact.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Why could not the government, through their commission, put a stipulation in the contract that no class of explosives could be used other than high-class explosives ? If that were done, it would settle the matter.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I think that if my hon. friend (Mr. Main) were a practical railway contractor, perhaps, he would not express himself in that way. It is a difficult thing to arrive at, for the examination of explosives might be a more difficult thing than was anticipated.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: If the minister's officers cannot ascertain these matters, how can he expect a country jury to ascertain them ? Does he expect them to take a crack at the explosive with a hammer V

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) is a great joker. But this is too serious a matter to talk about lightly. My hon. friend will see that a coroner's jury empanelled under the law, with the coroner taking evidence under oath, can summon the contractor, the manufacturer of the explosive, the seller of it, the men who have used some of the same explosives, and every 9ody else who can give information. They have every facility under the law to arrive at a conclusion.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Who pays the cost ol all these witnesses ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman knows that every province has now the machinery for these cases, including providing for costs. The question of provincial rights would be raised at once if we attempted to interfere with the duties of the provinces in this respect. The law of this province and every other province provides machinery to find where the blame rests. But I am making inquiry along these lines and will be able to make a statement, if I can get the information, which will clear the air. I agree that this is a very serious matter, one well worthy the attention of the department. I agree that the government should inquire into the reasons for these
accidents in order to learn how this loss of life is to be prevented or reduced.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: A somewhat similar condition existed in connection with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway so far as the hospital provision for the labourers on that railway were concerned. A very bad condition of affairs was shown to exist. Some kind of action was taken by the government and the abuses were corrected.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: That was on the Crows Nest Pass ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Yes. I am glad the minister says that he will intervene in this matter, because it is necessary that some high authority should intervene on behalf of these men. The contractors do not care for human life,-or that is too strong a way to put it ; I mean they have no financial interest other than burying these men who are killed. It would be a humane act on the part of the government to see to it that these men are surrounded with the necessary protection. If there is a reckless loss of life, the government should interfere and prevent it as far as possible.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
If there is any truth in this report-and I apprehend there is, because this is not the first case ofi the kind of which we have read t-it is quite evident that something! is wrong. There are other public works going on, on the Canadian Pacific Railway and on the Grand Trunk, under Larsen and Foley, where explosives are much more extensively used and in which such a state of facts does not exist and cannot exist. The Minister of Railways speaks of the protection afforded by the coroner's inquest as a means of making known the facts in these cases, but it is evident that this machinery is deficient, because this loss of life goes on continually and increasingly, according to what we have heard to-day. I must say I had no idea of it before, and I do not believe the people of the country had any idea of it either, but it is an intolerable condition. AVe have the Minister of Railways and also the Railway Commission, and these are the people most blameworthy for allowing this condition to continue. I am glad to hear that the Minister of Railways has stirred up the commission, but apparently he has not stirred them up enough. But we have another department that boasts of what it has done, and that is peculiarly in charge of the interest of the working people. I refer to the Labour Department. I have not heard that the Minister of Labour (Mr. Le-mieux) and his department has taken any interest in this question. Yet the settlement of it is a simple matter. In the first place, only proper explosives should be used ; and, in the second place, they should

be handled only by experienced people. No contractor should employ an inexperienced man for the handling of explosives, and no government should allow such a thing to be done. There is no need for using poor explosives, because there are so many excellent kinds that I cannot believe the contractor would purchase the inferior. But the fact remains that we have two departments and a railway commission directly interested and directly responsible and yet this terrible loss of life seems to go on and to increase. I think it is time that parliament said something about it and that the minister-both ministers-should move in the matter. It is well enough to speak of coroner's inquests, but where do the jurors in these inquests come from ? They are probably interested, or prejudiced or indifferent. I would not insinuate that these men would wilfully render improper verdicts, but if these inquests are held in places where there are no people except the workmen of the contractors, with the boss over them, that is enough reason for saying that an examination should be made by one of these departments to find out whether there is negligence in these cases. It ought to have been done before this time and it cannot be gone about too soon.

speakeroldname: Mr. JAMES CONMEE (Thunder Bay and Rainy River).
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
I think that the writer of the newspaper article which has been quoted here is not well posted as to how these accidents may possibly occur. They do not occur through the use of poor or bad explosives. I have had some experience in railway construction, and I am free to say that that has not been my experience. Speaking generally, it is admitted by all who have knowledge of the subject tha't the higher the explosive the more danger there is. Section B of the Canadian Pacific Railway parallels largely the poVtion of the Transcontinental Railway now under construction in the west for nearly 200 miles. In the construction of that section of the Canadian Pacific Railway glycerine oil was used, not dynamite, and accidents were more numerous. So when you come to add SO or 90 per cent of glycerine oil in dynamite, the danger is increased. Accidents occur under the most strict regulations, aud there are two or three causes for them. Carelessness is one great cause. But it is not always the inexperienced man who meets with an accident, it is very frequently the man of long experience who makes a mistake, notwithstanding that he ought to know better, and does know better, and ought to use more caution. But experienced men do make these mistakes. I think the history of railway construction will show that td be the case. I have had correspondence on this subject, having my attention lately drawn to it, and I took pains to make inquiry. I have written to a number of contractors whom I know and have received Mr. TISDALE.
some letters in reply. The hon. member for York (Mr. Maclean) stated that the contractors didn't care. I do not think that statement was warranted, it is very much out of place. I think the contractors do care. I think perhaps they have just as much honour and just as much feeling as other people have. Besides, they are deeply interested; accidents cause great loss to the contractors. Most of the contractors insure their men. I think you will find on inquiry that all the men under Mr. McArthur, or any prominent contractor I know of. are insured. Such contractors take precaution to have their men insured, by means of a small subscription monthly from the men themselves, which is supplemented by the contractor himself. So he is more or less interested. It is not quite fair to assume that he is not deeply interested or does not take all the precautions possible to be taken. I know of cases where the most strict regulations were in force, where notices were up in all the camps instructing men how to use dynamite in winter, telling them of the proper method of thawing it, as provided in water jacket cans. Notwithstanding that these strict regulations were in force, enforced as thoroughly as it was possible for the contractor to enforce them, and notifying every foreman and walking boss that if the rules were not enforced he would lose his position-notwithstanding all that, accidents have occurred, for the reason that men disobey these rules, and sometimes they get careless. Notv the hon. member who spoke last said there were not as many accidents on the Foley contract as on the Transcontinental. I think he is mistaken. The work is not of the same magnitude. There have been a great many accidents on that work. I know of two young men residents of Port Arthur who met death upon that particular work only a few months ago. The cause in that case was that the charge did not go off, and the men went back, as men sometimes do, to recharge, and the accident occurred. That is a cause of a good many accidents. Men become a little careless when the charge does not go off. These men I refer to were not labourers, they were contractors themselves; they did not send their workmen to run the risk, but they went themselves and took the risk. So it is a very hard matter to determine where responsibility lies. I quite agree with the hon. member that anything that can be done should be done to lessen the number of accidents. But it is a mistake to assume that the article in the newspaper is altogether warranted. The hon. gentleman spoke about the form of contract. I have run my eye over the present form of contract drawn up by the Transcontinental Railway Commission, and it does place all responsibility upon the contractor. He is bound to employ only competent men. The engineer in charge has power to dismiss any men on the works

666a
who are not competent for the duty entrusted to them. There is a very strict condition in the contract under which the work is done in regard to hospital accommodation. The contractor is bound to furnish hospital accommodation and medical attendance for the employees. So far as these matters can be provided for by the ordinary form of contract, they are provided for in this case. I am not taking the ground that something more should not be done. I do not know whether that could be done best by the Minister of Railways, or some official in his department, or whether it could be done best by the provincial authorities. But if anything can be done, certainly an effort should be made to minimize as far as possible the number of these unfortunate accidents.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
The loss of life in the construction of the Transcontinental Railway, so far as it has gone, has become a very serious matter. I think the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) has done a public duty in calling attention to it. The item he has read shows that 50 lives have been lost on one stretch of a hundred miles, or one on every two miles of that road, and it is not completed yet. I read a few weeks ago that eight men were killed by one explosion and several others injured upon that same stretch. We see that five men are dead and many others are mutilated for life by reason of these explosions that have taken place. They may have been premature, they may have been accidental, or they may have been the result of criminal carelessness. If the accidents were the result of any of these causes, certainly some one should be responsible. The country looks upon this railway, whether rightly or wrongly, as a government enterprise, a government work; the government are putting up the money to build the road, and the people look upon it as a government work. These contractors under the Transcontinental Railway Commission are certainly responsible to some one, and it should be the duty of the minister in the very near future to ascertain whether any precautions are being taken to preserve the lives of the men engaged on that arduous undertaking. We are too apt to say, Oh, they are only Italians, they are only navvies, they are no concern of ours. The ordinary feelings of humanity seem to be almost non-existent these days, because we read in almost every paper about the death of several workmen on some great work. Take the ' Evening Journal ' that has been quoted to-day, turn to page 7, there you will find a very sensible letter from an experienced contractor on this very point. I do not know who the writer is, I do not presume that he knew this question was coming up in the House to-day, or had anything to do with it. But he refers, not only to the death of these men in the west
upon this rock construction work, but also to the deaths that occurred on another branch of this Transcontinental Railway, that is the Quebec bridge. He makes the statement in that report that if ordinary precautions had been taken, if anybody with any experience had been on the spot, every life that was lost in the Quebec bridge accident could easily have been saved. He says that no man was justified in being on that work at least two or three days before the bridge fell and there was no one to warn the men on the bridge of the danger. There is another section which is responsible for the death of from SO to 90 persons-I forget the exact number, but it is not less than 80 and not more than 90. Up to this time the loss of life on this Transcontinental Railway has baffled all description in comparison with any other great work that has ever been undertaken in Canada. What is the reason of it? There must be some special reason. This article says that inexperienced men are employed. It said that in the old days when nitro-glycerine or dynamite was being used an experienced man was at the head of every gang and he was responsible. The writer says that they paid these men $4 or $5 a dav as bosses of these small gangs and every man acted like a soldier under the direction of the foreman in charge of the gang. A similar precaution should be taken in a case of this kind. Surely the government will not allow men to be sacrificed unnecessarily. We know that accidents will happen, we know that some lives will be lost in a great enterprise of this kind, but is it not unreasonable that fifty lives should be lost in the construction of 100 miles of rock road and that road is not completed yet. It certainly is out of proportion of the work done and if you take the Transcontinental Railway, 4,000 in length, I presume there will be 1,000 miles of hazardous work out of this 4,000. If they go on in the way that my hon. friend from Reel (Mr. Blain) has pointed out on that 1,000 miles you will have a loss of
1,000	or 2,000 lives before the road is completed, altogether too much of a sacrifice and not at all necessary. Where lives are lost and no one can prevent it we must view it as an act of Providence, but where men are ruthlessly slaughtered, as they are being to-day, we in this House have no right to keep silence on a point of that kind, and it is the duty of the government to see to it that the Transcontinental Railway Commission, or whoever are responsible, immediately do their duty and see that ordinary precautions are taken to preserve the lives of the workmen of Canada who are hazarding their lives in the building of this great national work. I trust that prompt action will be taken and that we will see a very large diminution in the future in the loss of life that we believe is unnecessarily taking place.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before tlie motion that you have put for the House to go into Committee of Supply is adopted, I desire to move an amendment on the lines that I announced some days ago, seconded by my hon. friend from Lennox (Mr. Uriah Wilson). The motion I have just placed in your hands, Mr. Speaker, is in the following terms:
While recognizing the importance of legitimate, well directed efforts to encourage desirable immigration, this House declares that it is time to cease paying a bounty at so much per head to agents for immigrants coming to Canada.
The total population of Canada, according to the last completed census, from information which 1 procured a day or two ago from the chief officer of statistics, Mr. Blue, is 5,371,315 souls. We are, therefore, Sir, considering the vast extent of our territory, a small community numerically and our country could, no doubt and will, support a far greater number of people. There is no congestion in Canada and all will and do, I am sure, agree that an increase of population in Canada is desirable. All must also readily agree that if an increase of population in this country is to accrue to us through immigration from other countries it is essential also that none but desirable persons should be admitted to Canadian citizenship and to the Canadian family. There is no immediate or urgent necessity for filling up the country. A few years more or less in the history of a young nation like ours are of very little account. In building up a nation and especially in merging large masses of foreign people, or even of elements not Canadian born, into the home population, I think that all of us will agree that too much precaution cannot be taken to secure the best elements, morally, mentally and physically to the end that what is imported into the nation will always be of the best, will readily conform to our customs and manners, and will arrive and be disseminated among our own people in such suitable proportions only as you can readily and without undue friction absorb. All this implies selection and the most careful selection. I think, we must admit. Face to face with the tendency to invade America, which is apparent to-day on all sides, from Europe, where an overcrowded population looks eagerly to this western hemisphere, as an Eldorado and a refuge, from the east, where a wave of Mongolians is beginning to surge towards our continent, the figures I will give will show that we will soon be overrun by an immigration which must become an element of large importance in our midst. If that element is not sound, if it does not conform to our recognized and wrell defined conditions our young nation will suffer great prejudice, and our advancement must be retarded by the arduous problems Mr. COCKSHOTT
which will be thrust upon us through our indifference and thoughtlessness.
The question is not a new one; it is a burning question in the United (States. We know that about twenty years ago it reached an acute stage in that cduntry. its immigration reports for the last few years show the truth of what I have just stated, that the question of immigration there presents to the people and to the consideration of the government one of the most formidable problems they have to deal with. It seems to me that in many respects the Americans have dealt with this question as a great nation face to face with this problem. Any one who reads the four last annual official reports of the United (States on immigration will very well realize the truth of what I have just stated: That they have allowed the tide of immigration to rise unduly and dangerously in their midst they themselves generally admit and it cannot be denied. They are seeking earnestly to-day to meet as best they can the serious national problems wdiich this has brought upon them. They have endeavoured to check and dam in a certain measure the rush of immigration to their shores. They have increased from time to time the head tax-a tax which is collected from each individual immigrant arriving in the country

they have forbidden for many years all and every aid to immigration in whatever shape, and they have set down restrictive conditions upon entry to their country. The federal government which, in the United States, is charged with the control of immigration, lias decided this year to send to Europe a commission, under section 39 of the law which was approved on February 20, 1907, still further restricting immigration. Niue of the most competent men to be found in the United States have been sent to travel in European countries whence immigration comes, and to acquire there all the information necessary for the United States to provide proper legislation with a view towards a solution of the problem which this question presents.
The motion of which 1 have given notice has been pending for some days and I have in the meantime collected from the official publications of the United .States government some figures which may interest the House. These figures I have procured with some trouble, and they are I believe absolutely reliable. I quote the following figures from the official report of the superintendent of immigration in the United States, showing the progress of the wave of immigration into that country :
Total immigration to United States for years mentioned.
Year ending June 30-
1904		  812,870
1905		 1,026,499
1906		 1,100,735
1907		 1,285,349
Total for four years	 4,225,453

Iu spite of the growing restrictive measures, and iu spite of the increased head tax on immigrants it will be seen that the immigration into the United States is increasing each successive year. The commissioner for immigration in the United States writes as follows in his last report for the year 1907, page 3, and which is the last report we have at hand :
An army of 1,285,349 souls that have come, drawn hither by the free institutions and the marvellous prosperity of our country; the chance here afforded for every honest toiler to gain a livelihood by the sweat of his brow or the exercise of his intelligence, surpassing in numbers the record of all preceding years. In the light of the past who can prophesy the future. The world can but view with wonder and awakening concern the facility with which we have absorbed the surplus millions of Europe and are now beginning to draw upon the reserve stock of some of these countries, and are even attempting to merge into our population some of the countless hordes of Asia.
I may say en passant that the United States immigration reports are far more ample and more detailed than a re the Canadian reports. It is impossible to go through any one of the United States reports for any given year without learning a multitude of very interesting facts, for which we look in vain in the Canadian reports; not only as to the increase in the number of immigrants, but what is far more important, as to their disposal when they reach the shores of the United States. I think our Department of Immigration could very well follow the example of the Immigration Department of the United States in the preparation of its immigration reports. And Sir. let me add that the 4.000.000 immigrants who came to the United States during the years 1904, 1905, 1906 and 1007, were brought to the United States without a single cent of expenditure by the American government, except that expense with regard to which there is no economy in the United States namely, the expense for inspection of immigrants and for the protection of the American people. There is inspection of the most minute character of all arriving in the United States and every precaution is taken to protect the nation from the influx of undesirables. So far ns I have been able to find not only from the official reports of the United States but from personal information sought by me in Montreal and in the United States itself, their inspection laws at present are well nigh perfect. Let me say also that this immigration has come to the United States in spite of the head tax upon the incoming immigrants which has produced in these four years the following results :
United States head tax on immigrants. Head tax collected on immigrants entering
the United States-
1904	$1,599,472 25
1905	 2,032,873 50
1906	 2,290,901 56
1907	 2,782,103 68
Total collected for four years	 8,755,350 94
This sum was more than ample to provide a perfect service of inspection and to leave a large balance at the end of each year to the credit of the American government. Now, as I have said, the law in the United States debarring immigrants is very strict and I may mention that the total number of debarred immigrants from the year 1892 to the year 1904, was 47,768. For the four years for which I have already given statistics the number of immigrants debarred from entering the United States was as follows :
Immigrants debarred from entering the United States.
1904		 7,994
1905		 11,879
1906		 12,432
1907		 13,034
These figures are taken from the official reports published by the United States Department of Commerce and Labour. Another feature of the question to which I would call the attention of the House and which is of deep interest to us at the present time, and which must daily become of greater moment, is that feature of the American law which obliges each immigrant landing iu the United States to be in possession of a certain sum of money. They consider it a safe provision to absolutely oblige the immigrants to be provided with sufficient funds to maintain themselves and their families upon their arrival in the Republic. Let us see the effect of this law-or regulation in the four years for which I have given the figures. Under the operation of this resolution, the following amounts of money were brought into the United States by immigrants, as certified by the officers of inspection.
1904		$20,894,383
1905		 25,159,012
1906		 25,109,413
1907		 25,599,893
That is, in those four years something like $100,000,000 of cash, apart from goods and effects, have been brought by immigrants into that country. This is an item of some importance because I feel that in this respect our law is not sufficient. It is true that under the stress from which we have suffered lately we have temporarily required that immigrants must have with them a certain sum of money, $50 I think during the winter, reduced on April 1, to $25 or entirely discontinued. It is evident that we must amend our regulations more in accordance with the American system if we are to secure in Canada a larger number of people than we are now securing who are able to support themselves after reach-

ing our shores, so that we shall avoid the experience of last winter.
I have deemed it important to place these figures before the House and their preparation has required some care and research. I shall now come to matters more directly affecting our own country. In the American reports we find valuable information as to the immigrants who have reached the United States from Europe through Canada.
In 1904, 30,374 immigrants entered the United States in this way. In that year 2,100 who attempted to enter the United States through Canada from Europe were debarred on account of the laws and regulations of the United States and therefore had to remain in Canada. Of these 762 were paupers, 582 were suffering from loathsome disease, and 293 were prostitutes.
in 1905 the total immigration to the United States through Canada amounted to 44.264, an increase of more than 14,000 over that of the preceding year. The United States, in 1905, finding that the immigrants coming through Canada were very numerous, and finding also, as appears by the four reports to which I have referred, that our own laws in respect to immigration were extremely defective, incomplete and lacking in regard to causes of exclusion and their application, adopted regulations providing the immigrants arriving in the United States through Canada into more than one class. Thus, in that year, we find the 44,264 arriving in the United States through Canada divided into three classes.
(a)	Those destined to the United States landed at Canadian ports.
(b)	Those arriving in Canada from Europe and proceeding to the United States within a year, and
(c)	Those destined for Canada who after the expiry of a year proceeded to the United States.
Of those arriving at Canadian ports with the avowed and declared intention of going to the United States there were 12,663 and 183 were debarred. What became of them when they were debarred at our Canadian ports I do not know, it is impossible to find any trace of their disposition. Were they sent back to Europe in the vessels in which they came to Canada ? I doubt it very much. If, on the contrary, they did land and proceeded without examination to one of the examining stations on the Canadian frontier and were there debarred, I doubt very much if they were deported back to Europe.
The second class are those destined to Canada and who have gone to the United States within a year after their arrival in this country. They have to submit to examination at one of the numerous examining stations which the United States government have established along the border, on the ground that we admitted a great many undesirables who found their way into the Mr. MONK.
United States. After having made representations to the Canadian government on that subject which to a large extent the American Commissioners admit have been carried out, still they have found it necessary to establish these posts of examination. In the second class of immigrants we find 8517 and 589 were debarred. I shall not go into the details of the causes of their exclusion from the United States, many were refused admission for those causes which were causes of exclusion from Canada and how they succeeded in entering Canada I do not know. Nor do I know what became of them when they were refused admission to the United States. It is impossible to trace the matter any further, but my own view is that they remained in Canada, and that we have to-day in Canada these immigrants who were deemed undesirables under the American law for pronounced and stated causes.
We have to-day in Canada these immigrants who are deemed undesirable under the American law and pronounced so from causes which no doubt really existed, judging by the thorough examination made by American officers. These undesirables we have in Canada. My hon. friend from Beauharnois (Mr. Bergeron) asks if we paid a bonus on these immigrants. No doubt we did. No doubt they came within the classes, so very extensive and comprehensive, upon which we pay bonuses. Where these people are to-day I do not know, but they were found absolutely unfit for admission into the United States. 8,000 of them were not refused entry into the United States. On these no doubt the government paid a bonus. Why should they not ? If these people were booked from England or any other country in which we grant a bonus to immigrants of certain classes- very comprehensive classes-the booking agent got his bonus on them, when they came here, and they afterwards went to the United States. There is a third class and that is those who were destined to Canada and who went to the United States after the expiry of a year. Here we have a still more doubtful case. After the year expired-how long after we do not know- they went to the United States. That is a very large class indeed. They numbered in 1905, according to the official report, 19,308, of which were debarred 749 ; and the remarks I made in connection with the second class apply with still greater force to this class.
I wish to anticipate an objection which will probably be made by my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver). After it became evident that a very large number of these immigrants went off to the United States within the year or after the year had expired, the Department of the Interior, through the initiative of the American officers-that was when we were under the unfortunate and mysterious regime

of the North Atlantic Trading Company- arranged with the head office of the American Immigration and Inspection Department in Montreal, where all the returns from these border stations along the Canadian frontier are made before they are forwarded to Washington, to have returns made to the Department of the Interior of those immigrants who, after having come to Canada, went off to the United States. I presume the object of that-I think that was shown by one of the officers of the department under examination in the Committee on Agriculture and Colonization- was -to find out what percentage of these continental immigrants, upon whom we paid these very large sums as a bonus to the North Atlantic Trading Company, went to the United States. What resulted from that I do not know. I remember examining at some length an officer of the department in the committee, and he there said that these reports were sent to the Department of the Interior, and that before the accounts were settled with the North Atlantic Trading Company they had some means of tracing these immigrants forwarded through the instrumentality of that company and striking off those who went to the United States. Whether that was ever done I do not know. Whether that arrangement is continued to this day I do not know. Probably the Minister of the Interior can tell us, but I do not think it has been kept up, and I do not think we are in a position to say exactly what becomes of our bonused immigrants after they reach here and what proportion go to the United States. I do not think we have a system of proper cheek, and there must be an immense leakage, because the temptation of the immigrant is very great to go to the United States once he arrives here. And although the government, in face of the continued increasing tide of immigration, has improved the law or at least carried out more carefully the inspection, there is no doubt whatever that in Europe the impression prevails among booking agents and others interested and the migratory population in general, that it is much easier to get into Canada than into the United States. Therefore those who are objectionable are generally attracted towards Canada. If the House desired to go further into the question, I could quote extensively from the very able report of Inspector Braun, who was sent from the United States in 1903 to survey the whole field of immigration, and he gives, in regard to that tendency, very valuable information to his government. He says there are people from some of the easterly countries of Europe, doubtful, objectionable people, who are directed to the great ports of embarkation, and who are given signals which they carry with them, indicating that they are not likely to obtain entry into the United States and therefore are to be directed to Canada. That exist-212
ed to a very large extent until we made our laws more severe, but at the time Inspector Braun made his report, this abuse was very extensive.
Turning again to immigration, in 1905, 800 were debarred as likely to become public charges. I think they remained in Canada. I see no way whatever by which they could have been reconveyed, having been once admitted, to the sea-board and deported to Europe. Out of these 800 there were 492 ,who were debarred as suffering from trachoma. I have already had occasion to refer to that very dangerous disease which exists in a chronic state in the southern and eastern parts of Europe. It is, at certain stages, incurable and extremely infectious. Two or three years before there were 600 debarred from entering the United States through Canada on account of trachoma, and these have remained in Canada as well as the 492 first mentioned. The last time I spoke on this subject I snoke of the able report of one of our Montreal specialists, in which he gave the proof that trachoma had been treated at the Montreal General Hospital. The House knows we have a trachoma hospital at Quebec to which immigrants are taken who suffer from that disease. Too much care cannot be taken because once this disease has taken firm hold it will be practically impossible to eradicate it.
Let me give a few figures of the total immigration in 1906. The total emigration from Canada to the United States was 43,997. We have no detailed report as to the three classes to which I have referred. There were 486 debarred of which 331 are likely to become public charges.
In 1907 we have again an increase of immigration through Canada to the United
States :
By Atlantic ports	 18,671
Through border	statioji	 20,882
Pacific ports	 1,414
Total	 48,967
Out of which were debarred 2,273.
It is impossible to find in our own reports anything to even remotely indicate an answer to that very interesting question as to what becomes of these numerous people who were debarred from entering the United States after having come to Canada. In the American reports you will find answers to all these questions. You will find absolutely reliable information as to the number of people who leave the United States within the year. They give us comprehensive statements as to the immigration to the United States.
It must be evident that we require tint information. We require to know parti u-larly who are the people going out. What about the large numbers of people who come to our country and then go to the United States ? The question was put to my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior, and he was asked why we had not that in-
