speechtext:
formation. He answered because that concerned emigration and not immigration. It must be evident that our information regarding immigration is incomplete, in view of the bonuses and the money we spend on immigration. Our data are not sufficient unless we have what is given in the United States, and that is the amount of people who leave Canada after coming there.
Tlte total number for the year 1907 of the immigrants to United States through Canada was 48,967. Besides these 2,273 were debarred from entering the United States.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: They may be in Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
No doubt. There are no tables in the general report beyond those from which I have culled the information which I have just given the House, but the Canadian Commissioner for the United States, a very able man who was in charge of that branch and administered the whole Canadian service connected with immigration through Canada to the United States, says at page 85 of the United States Immigration Report for 1907 :
The tables above mentioned however contain other data however, upon which I am prompted to feel the bureau will not look with such satisfaction reference being had to the unusual increase of the number of aliens who originally giving Canadian destinations proceeded to the United States within one year from date of arrival in Canada. From 9,721 during fiscal year ended June 30, 1906, this class has increased to 15,677 for the year just closed. This lemarkable increase is partially explained by the fact that while less than -60 per cent of these manifested to the United States at time of embarkation are excluded more than 10-06 per cent of the year in Canada class, find it impossible to meet the requirements of our laws when examined.
Only -60 per cent of those manifested to the United States were excluded, but when we come to those who pass into the United States after being manifested through Canada, you find an immense increase in the proportion exclude namely 10-06 per cent. That strengthens the conviction that the immigrants are shipped, even to-day, to Canada direct when there is some doubt of their admissibility into the United States. I deemed it important to give these data to the House because the question of immigration is one which demands our immediate attention.
I have stated enough respecting the American immigration features which concern us, let me refer now to our own system. What are the causes of exclusion from Canada? They are to be found in chapter 93 of the Revised Statutes of Canada. These are the immigrants prohibited, under the provisions of this law, as it has since been amended, and amended a great deal on the representations made from time to time by the American authorities.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
1.	Feeble-minded, idiotic, paralytic and insane persons. Deaf, dumb, blind or infirm persons, unless accompanied by family or persons to take care of them. This is under the amendment of the-law made by 6 Edward VII., chapter 19.
2.	Immigrants afflicted with loathsome contagious or infectious diseases which may be dangerous to public health or widely disseminated, unless curable within a reasonably short time.
3.	Paupers, vagrants, beggars or those likely to become a public charge may be deported if they become a public charge within two years of their arrival.
4.	Criminals, prostitutes and procurers.
There are boards of inquiry who hear appeals made from the decision of the inspector. This, I think, has been the case only since the law of last year or the year before. I think these boards of inquiry, which sit very frequently in the United States .have not been called upon to act here very often. I say that subject to correction by my hon. friend. There is also a final appeal to. the minister. There is one provision of the law that may usefully be pointed out and that is not generally known. It is that the immigrant who has been convicted of crime or has become a public charge within two years of his arrival here, may, upon a certificate notifying the minister to that effect from the clerk of the municipality where he has become a public charge or been convicted, may be ordered by the minister to deportation. I say that that clause is not familiar to the people of this country, for, within the last seven or eight months undoubtedly, a great many immigrants have become public charges in the municipalities of Canada. I can speak with certainty concerning the case of Montreal.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: How about the Douk-hobors ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: That law' would not apply to them now', because when the Doukhobors came in this provision did not exist. But look at the number of immigrants w'ho have been convicted of offences, both petty and extremely grave, within the limits of Montreal alone and within the past year. They would come under this provision of the law as well as if they had become public charges on the fact being certified to the Minister of the Interior that he has pow'er to deport them.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: At w'hose expense?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
That is a question I desire to refer to briefly. Suppose that an immigrant has reached the w-est, and is to be deported. He must be brought to the port of embarkation at the country's expense. He must be sent, and a man with him, at the expense of the country, and traces of these expenditures are found in our public accounts. He is taken to the port of embarkation, and only there is he handed over to the steamship company. And I find re-
6G73

' cords of moneys paid to steamship companies in connection with deportation-I do not know under what circumstances. But, under the law, the steamship company is obliged to take the immigrant back.
It would be very interesting-to come more close to the subject of the motion I have placed in your hands-to find out how the system of paying so much per head for immigrants .first started in this country. It was started very long ago. I believe that inquiry would unquestionably reveal the fact that this singular, this almost unheard-of, mode of recruiting for our national family was invented and urged upon the government by transportation companies, booking agents and employees connected with the department. It is impossible for me to think that a man having at heart the interests of the country, and totally dissociated from the interests to which I have referred-great, powerful and influential interests-could ever have believed that a scheme of paying so much a head per immigrant, was a suitable, feasible and wise method for a country to follow that was desirous of increasing the national family by the addition of good, suitable and carefully selected subjects.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: It is only within eleven years, is it not?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
I think this system dates further back than that. Of course, when our immigrants were very few, when we spent from $20,000 to $100,000 on immigration, though the bonusing system may have existed, it amounted to a negligible quantity. But to-day, when we spend over $1,000,000 on immigration, a large portion of it in bonuses, it becomes an important question to find out who invented this method. If you wanted to increase a valuable herd of cattle, you would not adopt the sole principle of paying so much per head. When it is a question of the national family, and adding to it in the immense proportions which will appear in a moment, that principle seems to me a very bad one. Certain it is that it has existed for many years, but as I have stated, it has only been of large and alarming proportions since 1898, since which time it has become a subject of study. As I stated before, I do not think anybody would adopt such a principle even in an effort to increase a herd of animals. Remember, the party earning the bonus is bound by no strict rule. The rule that binds him is only that he gets his immigrant through the cursory examination that takes place upon the arrival of the immigrants here. If his immigrant is deported -though it is not so stated in any of the regulations I have seen-the presumption is be would not earn his bonus. But no code of stringent rules has been laid down for him. With respect to this, I may quote from a report brought down at the instance of file lion, member for Lennox (Mr. Uriah 2121
Wilson) by the Minister of the Interior oil Thursday, February 13, 1908, in which is to be found very valuable information in regard to this and other points. The agent is not called upon, for instance, to make any special examination. He is not called upon to make any special selection. He knows upon wThat immigrants we pay bonuses, and there is nothing in any of the regulations I have seen that obliges them to exercise careful, prudent discretion in the selection of immigrants. He is not bound to see who this gentleman is whose destination is Canada, and to be added to the Canadian national family. No duty is imposed upon him to look into the man's record. He may be a criminal. Of course if he is a convicted criminal, that is found out, but it is very difficult to find it out, but when found out it may prevent his landing. There is no duty imposed upon the booking agent, or the man who earns the bonus, to look into the history of the incoming immigrant. He is not called upon to procure any certificate to show that this man is not a scoundrel or a loafer, a class that every nation in Europe is anxious to get rid of. There is nothing in the regulations which binds the booking agent to guarantee that this man is an honest or a suitable man to be admitted to Canada.
An bon. MEMBER. The American law.
Mi-. MONK. Under the American law there is no bonus, there is no immigration agent, and never has been. They would not think of such a thing as paying a bonus on immigrants. I am pointing out the situation of this agent over in Europe who earns the bonus, and showing that he is not in any way responsible for the character of the immigrant. He has to pay no fine when he ships over to this country, as he often does, unsuitable and undesirable men. He is subject to no penalty, though the immigrant that he sends out here may be debarred as a pauper, a criminal, or likely to become a burden. As a matter of fact, this agent who earns the bonus can not be reached by us because he is not under our jurisdiction. I know as a matter of fact that the booking agents in Europe, and even in England, I know it from reliable information, frequently know nothing about Canada except what they may have picked up from circulars. Half of them do not know about the conditions of labour here. I am speaking of the booking agent, the man who gets ttie money. Let any man go to Europe and interview these men, and he will find that they know nothing about Canada, and as a matter of fact they care nothing about Canada, and have no interest in this country. They simply tell the immigrant, All you have to say, if you want to get into Canada, is that you are a farm hand or a railway navvy. Many times the immigrant does not know the language of the country, either French or English, but

he is carefully taught to say ' farm hand ' or ' railway hand ' when met by the inspecting officer. Frequently these people arrive in great numbers in port, and when an inspector has to pass a thousand of them, what is he going to do ? Look into the mouth of every one of them? Examine his conscience? He has to pass a thousand in an hour or two, the train is under steam waiting to take them west, and everybody is in a rush. Let any man go down and witness the arrival of these immigrants. Probably they could not understand you if you spoke to them in French or English. Now I have made a rather hazardous assertion, Mr. Speaker, and that is that this extraordinary policy of giving so much per head to immigrants, under the circumstances to which X have referred, has been initiated by the transportation companies.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: When ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: In the origin, probably. What my right hon. friend wishes me to say is that it was originated under the Conservative government.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
I do not care about that.
Mr. ARMAND LAVERG-NE. Would that be a reason for us to change it ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: It would be a reason for us to change it, though I do not consider that the sins of the fathers should be visited upon the sons beyond the third and fourth generation. But I find no trace of its origin anywhere else. You have the transportation companies pressing upon the government, and they are very influential, to adopt this scheme. It is to their interest. You have the booking agent who makes representations to our immigration staff, and the immigration staff itself, ns has been proved in relation to the North Atlantic Trading Company, was at one time at least deeply interested in immigration. But to-day you have, in addition, the influence of these large land owners in the Northwest who are greatly interested in increasing population. So you have three distinct interests. You have the interest of the transportation companies, which is immense. Let the House consider for a moment how a large transportation company makes money out of the immigrant, from the moment they get hold of him. The immigrant as a rule pays $27 to the company to take him across the Atlantic. I suppose 25 cents per day pays for his food and the space he occupies on board the steamer. The food is simple and bought in large quantities, and the immigrant is often seasick. At any rate, an investigation wlil establish that 15 or 20 cents a day will pay for his food, and 25 cents a day will pay for all the cost in bringing him across the Atlantic. He has paid the company $27. The moment he lands here the transportation company conveys him to the west. He arrives in the west, and gives value to the1

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
land owned by these transportation companies. Sometimes he buys the land, at any rate, his mere arrival adds value to the land. Then on everything he buys in order to live, the transportation companies reap a profit; that is to say, the boots he wears, and the clothes on his back, and the food he eats are all freighted to the Northwest by these transportation companies.
I say that, with the immense profits this immigration gives to these companies, they are immensely interested in the maintenance of the status quo in regard to our law respecting immigration. Now Sir, in confirmation of that, let me say that it must strike the House as a rather singular fact that, after the disappearance of the North Atlantic Trading Company in 1906, by order in council of the 19th February, 1907, the bonus was fixed at ten shillings per adult and six shillings for children. That was on the 19th February, 1907, at a time when we had ceased to do business with the North Atlantic Trading Company, and it had been found absolutely necessary, I may say, in response to public opinion, to cancel that contract. On the Cth January, 1908, less than a year afterwards, the government increase and double that bonus. Why is the bonus on the territory covered by the North Atlantic Trading Company increased and doubled? It is impossible to understand why the order in council of this year doubling the continental bonus was passed. There is a pretext alleged in the order and it is that the bonus is found inadequate to induce immigration. That is the textual reason given in the order. Let us see if there is any foundation for that allegation which was the basis of that new order in council doubling the amount of the bonus. In the year ending the 30th June, 1906, we had 189,064 immigrants. In the year ending the 30th June, 1907, we had 252,038 immigrants. In the year in which we have 252,038 immigrants, with a very large increase in continental immigration, we increase and double the continental bonus. Let me give the precise amount of that increased continental immigration. For nine months to the 30th March, 1906, the number of continental immigration was 19,216. For the nine months to the 30th March, 1907, it was 34,217, an increase of 15,001, and in the following three months the increase was greater still. I see see no reason here for increasing and doubling the continental bonus. Although the North Atlantic Trading Company as such has disappeared, has dropped out of existence, I think that anybody who carefully examines our system of immigration and the way the propaganda is carried on at present will conclude that there exists several North Atlantic Trading Companies, combinations, I mean, of booking agents, of people interested in immigration and in getting the bonuses. There is not only one. It has been a fecund institution, it

was very prosperous and it produced numerous offspring. Let us look for a moment at the conditions which have surrounded our increase of population by immigration since 1898. After a careful examination of this
tabulated statement, compiled from absolutely reliable official sources, controlled by the officers of the department, the House will see clearly and exactly the trend of the wave of immigration since 1898.

I may say that a large proportion of the bonuses for continental immigrants went to the North Atlantic Trading Company.
One word now to make clear what the present regime as to bonusing is under the regulations or orders in council at this moment in force. The bonuses paid at the present time are as follows:
United States.-Since 1897 a bonus has been paid to sub-agents of $3 on each man,
$2 on each woman and $1 on each child, of the farming class from the United States. In a few cases the commission is $2, $1 and 50 cents on men, women and children of specified classes.
British.-£1 sterling on adults, 10 shillings on those between 1 and 18 years of age who come to Canada to engage in farm work, railway work or, in the case of females, domestic service, who are British

subjects by birth or naturalization and who have had at least one year's experience as farmers, farm labourers, gardeners, stablemen, carters, railway surfacemen, navvies or miners.
Iceland.-A bonus of £1 on full tickets and 10 shillings on half tickets is allowed to steamship companies on immigrants from Iceland, through an arrangement with the steamship companies that the rate or passage to immigrants is decreased by that amount.
Continental.-A bonus of £1 on adults and 10 shillings on those between 1 and 18 years of age is paid to certain selected booking agents in Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Holland, Germany, Finland, France and Belgium on immigrants from those countries who come to Canada to engage in farm work and who, before coming to Canada, had at least one year's experience in one of the prescribed occupations. These are the same as in the case of the British immigrants.
In fact, after the description I have given to the House as to how the immigration is started on the other side by the agent, and how the immigrant is received here, I think it is evident that almost anybody can get in under these regulations, because we have no way of verifying the statement made by the immigrant to the inspector here. The immigrant is not required to produce any proof of any statement he may make, and he is allowed to pass into the country on his assertion that he is a farm hand, a railway navvy, a gardener or a stableman. And, to those who have witnessed large numbers of immigrants on their arrival here passing before the inspector it is impossible not to say that a great number of these immigrants have it written on their faces that they have never been farmers or railway navvies. The agent can do nothing to prevent them under the circumstances I have narrated; he has to take their statements. Under the order in council of January last (1908) the bonus was doubled from that which it was under the order in council of February, 1907, and that was done without any reason that I can see, the pretext given that there was a falling off in the immigration being absolutely unfounded as shown by the statistics I have given to the House. It is not out of place to remark that according to the answer given by the Minister of the Interior and reported in 1 Hansard ' of the 16th of March last, we have spent to date on immigrant hospitals a total sum of $208.420.63. I quote this in connection with the statement which is sometimes made that Immigration to this country is not assisted. T will refer to that later on, but in the meantime I will point out that we have spent over $200,000 in providing hospitals which are simply for immigrants only.

subtopic: STATEMENT SHOWING THE AMOUNT OF BONUSES PAID ON IMMIGRANTS TO CANADA FROM JULY 1, 1897, TO DECEMBER 31, 1907.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had no idea when I began that the observations I had to make would take up so much time. Perhaps my right hon. friend the Prime Minister is not wholly free from a responsibility for this, as when I first gave notice of this motion I expected to bring it up at an early date and since that notice was given, a great many people in my own province particularly, who take a deep interest in this question have sent me much of the information I am now giving to the House. I had determined to sift and prune that information as much as possible, but I found when proceeding with the expurgatorial work that it was more difficult than I had at first imagined. Most of these data I think are important in the examination of this or any other question connected with immigration.
When you left the chair at six o'clock I was stating that it was a question of very great interest whether or not we in Canada got the benefit of this bounty or bonus expenditure. Do we not pay for Immigrants who come to Canada and within a year or after a year proceed to the United States ? I expressed very serious doubts as to that and these doubts will be confirmed by what lam about to say to the House. Bonuses, as I understand, are paid monthly and once paid I doubt if we ever get them back. Is there any instance of a bonus, after once being paid, having been recovered because the immigrant, either within the year or after the year left for the United States or because he was deported after a certain time by reason of becoming a public charge? I do not think the minister can give any example of a refund having been made by the bonused agent of the bonus he has received. I do not think we would have any right to that refund. Once the immigrant has entered Canada and been accepted by the inspecting authorities, the bonus appears to me, by what I have seen of the regulations, to have been earned. The agent is entitled to it and it is impossible to recover it from him, whatever circumstances may afterwards supervene.
I find in one of our Quebec papers, the Richmond ' Guardian,' an article which I feel bound to give to the House, which affords ground for seriously doubting whether all this vast mass of immigration comes to Canada, whether they really go to people the Northwest or to improve our own population in, the older provinces. This article appears in the Richmond ' Guardian ' of February 21, 1908, and reads as follows :
The Interior Department gives out glowing reports of increased immigration. These statements are clearly false. About half the settlers reported can never be found after-

ward. This is proved by the Northwest census of 1906, which shows the population of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta to be
as follows:
1906	 808,863
1901	 419,512
Increase	 389,351
Returns of births and deaths make the natural increase of the population of 1901 41,951, leaving 347,400 to be supplied from outside, and by the natural increase of these immigrants. Now the number of homestead settlers in the Northwest from other provinces in the five years is represented by the department to be 27,625. The department counts two and a half persons for each homesteader, making 69,312 inhabitants from this source.
A much larger number from the older provinces settled on lands which they purchased, or in towns and villages, or were employed in the various works and industries of the country. This would leave less than 200,000 to be supplied by immigrants and their children.
Note now the number of immigrant settlers reported by the department as having located in Manitoba, Alberta and Saskatchewan in the five years preceding the June, 1906:
1901-	2.. .. 61,129 see Interior report, page 99.
1902-	3.. ..109,986 see Interior report, page 95.
1903-	4.. .. 75,308 'Hansard,' 1906-7, page 1053.
1904-	5.. .. 74,676 'Hansard,' 1906-7, page 1053.
1905-	6.. .. 90,652 'Hansard,' 1908-7, page 1053.
Total. .411,652
Here are more than twice as many immigrants reported to have settled in the west as could be found there by the census enumerators. The number of immigrant settlers reported from 1901 to 1906 is 22,301 more than the total increase of population from all sources.
What has become of the 200,000 or 250,000 lost people? This includes the 22,301 mentioned above, also the total natural increase of the oldest settlers, and of the immigrants, themselves, together with all that arrived from the older provinces and their descendants. Either these 200,000 never came or they came and went away. On how many of these imaginary immigrants did the country pay a bonus of $4 and $5 per head? On how many did the mysterious North Atlantic Trading Company draw $5 for each imaginary head? How many of them were travellers coming into the country and going out by another or the same gate? How many were Canadian travellers coming home? How many were picnickers from across the borders? How many were mere dead figures stuffed into the books to make glory for the Immigration Department, gain for the immigration contractors, and excuse for an annual immigration expenditure which has jumped from $120,000 to $950,000 since the change of government?
But, Sir. there are other figures that go to show that our Northwest lands, which we are so desirous of seeing settled by real bona fide farmers are not being settled in the way the immigration returns would lead us to expect. Let me give briefly a statement showing what proportion ofi our immigrants go upon the free lands of the Northwest, the increase in the number of homestead entries, the total immigration and the percentage of the homestead increase to the total immigration for'each year from 1896 until the present.

There is therefore grave reason to doubt that we are really getting in our Northwest Territories the benefit of Jill this bonus expenditure.
One word as to the incompleteness of the immigration report. There is nothing in it to show the movement through Canada into the United States of the Immigrants either on arrival or within the year or after the year. The reason given for that omission by the Minister of the Interior on the 16th of March last was that this exodus was emigration and not Immigration. Nevertheless although the United States do not bonus immigrants or aid immigration in any way, they give information in their report which shows the exodus of people from the United States, so that in this connection our report, as compared with the American report, is scanty to a degree.
I find that the reports from seaports in the British isles are no fuller, since the tide of immigration has increased, than they were before. The report from our Belgium agent is always couched in the same terms. It is almost identically the same every year. And from the continent we get no report at all. We get, of course* from the Superintendent General of Immigration some very general observations, but no details. That is a serious fault which the minister ought to try and remedy. In the United States we maintain agencies which cost us from $2,000 to $6,000 a year and even more. How is it that we do not find in the last report of the Department of the Interior any state-

meut whatever from these agents? Surely when we pay them so much money, we ought to be informed in detail what each of these immigration agents is doing and what bonuses are paid them so that we may know that they are earning their money.
Before you left the Chair, Sir, I was pointing out that this immigration business is an extremely profitable one for the transportation companies, the booking agents, and those individuals and companies who are interested in large tracts of land in the Northwest. The transportation companies not only make a large profit out of the fares, not only do they afterwards draw profit from the immigrant when he lands, but they undergo no expense in putting the immigrant on board or in landing him. An immigrant is not like ordinary freight. He goes on board of his own accord, there is no machinery or labour required to put him on board, and when he reaches his destination there is no expense in putting him ashore, and he is then taken charge of by the government. Although it is said that we do not assist immigration, we have gone to great expense in building sheds and hospitals, in taking charge of the quarantine, in paying all the expenses of inspection, and in providing every description of necessaries for the immigrant when he lands. We feed him, we see to his safe transference in his destination, and incur considerable expense in that work. More-ever, we do the advertising for these transportation companies. We spend immense sums every year to advertise this country and to induce immigrants to come here. In fact, the transportation companies have no expense in connection with this branch of their business, though in every other they must incur large expenses.
One word as to the bonused agent himself. This agent receives a commission from the transportation company on the ticket he sells to the immigrant. That commission varies. As the immigrant must practically always go to some inland place away from the port of debarkation, the agent receives a further commission for his transportation. He probably gets a commission from parties who employ the immigrant on his coming to this country. I take it that the amount he makes on each immigrant, including the $5 of bonus which we give him, must amount to $10 or $12 at the very least. If he handles any considerable number of immigrants. his profits must be even abnormally large. Even if he were deprived of the bonus given by the Dominion government, the commissions to which I have referred and the salary he gets as booking agent would show a considerable profit for each immigrant he handles. As a rule the booking agents in the British islands and even elsewhere, are engaged in some general business, as dealing in coal or some other occupation. The agent, as a rule, is not well versed in the country to which he is Mr. MONK.
sending immigrants. That explains why so many immigrants have been left to public support during last winter. The agent will tell the immigrant, for instance, that he knows that farm-hands in Canada earn from $45 to $60 a month. That is not absolutely untrue, for I am told that in the west, during harvest time-and even in other provinces-large salaries are paid to good farm hands. But their employment at these rates lasts for only a short time. The immigrants, however, are not informed of that; and, frequently, when they arrive in Montreal, where many of them are stranded, they will not work except for a considerable salary, for they have been told not to accept work unless paid at about the rate I have stated.
In regard to the class of immigrants who arrive here, let me give to the House what Lord Stratheona says in this year's report of the Department of the Interior:
Another serious matter to which I have drawn the attention of the imperial authorities is that magistrates and others have repeatedly deferred passing judgment on transgressors against the law, on the condition of their being sent to Canada.
I have, from time to time, had direct correspondence with recorders, chairmen of sessions, and others, whenever a particular case of the kind came under my notice, formally and emphatically condemning such action. Attention has also been widely drawn to the views of your department on the matter in the press of this country, and I hoped, as a consequence, no further causes of complaint would arise.
In view, however, of the two further cases which you recently brought to my attention, I felt compelled to make official representations to His Majesty's government on the subject. These negotiations are still pending, but I hope they may lead to steps being taken which will put a stop altogether to countenance being given by magistrates and others concerned to the sending of persons convicted of crime to Canada.
I think that abuse has not ceased. And. to be perfectly frank, the general impression which exists in the British islands is that the people there do us a favour by sending out the unemployed and those who cannot get on in the old country. I do not speak against immigrants as a whole, for some are excellent and are a great acquisition. But the impression that I have spoken of exists in the British islands and they do not hesitate to state it. There is an impression that this is a country of enormous resources, immense areas of fertile lands that are given away, and that it is an advantage to pour out population into this country and that there will always be found something for newcomers to do; even though they may have been found incapable of getting on in the older countries. I am told that an eminent writer, recently in Canada, Mr. Rudyard Kipling, has written that we

must pump the Britishers into this country. We are glad to receive Britishers in Canada, for many of them make excellent immigrants. But we ought to accept only the best class, and there are undesirable classes in England as elsewhere. As a matter of fact, I think the magistrates of Montreal will bear me out when I say that, during the past seven or eight months, most of those who have been brought before our courts of justice for serious offences are not men of this country, but immigrants who have slipped in in one way or other. Judges who preside at our assizes, I think, would report to the government, if questioned, and the magistrates have repeatedly told me, that this is the condition of affairs in Montreal. As a matter of fact, to-day, it is almost impossible for our country people without danger to follow the custom which, for all time, has existed among them, of coming to the Montreal market during the night. Up to within two years ago, farmers-and not farmers only but their wives and even their children-would dome on their carts during the night to Montreal to be on the market early in the morning, without any thought of danger on the public highway leading into the city. In Montreal we preserve the peace with a very small proportion of police protection, but this has become impossible because of outrages committed on the public roads leading to Montreal. People have been held up, assaulted, wounded and left to die on the public highway. And there is no doubt in the mind of anybody that these outrages have not been committed by our own people; they are committed by immigrants who are stranded in Montreal. Cases of that kind have been discovered and the perpetrators belong to the foreign criminal classes undoubtedly. Let me read a paragraph from the last report of the inspector of hospitals for the province of Ontario:
There is marked evidence that public attention should be called to the large number of undesirable and unsuitable immigrants that are being induced to seek a shelter in Ontario. This has been found nowhere more noticeable than in the city of Toronto, where more than half of the indigent casuals, who have had to be provided for, belong to the immigrant class. In many instances, however, they prove quite incapable and, when winter comes on, they drift into the cities and are not slow to find the location of the charitable institutions. The whole fault for this condition must be placed where it belongs, namely, in the system that permits and encourages immigration without a proper discrimination. The present policy of Canadian emigration agents in Europe would seem to be to secure the number and pay no heed to the quality of persons urged to seek a haven in this country. The system of the Dominion government of bonusing agents to send out in an apparently indiscriminate raaner a class of people totally unfit to provide a livelihood for themselves is deplorable. During the past year it has cost the hospitals and public charities of Ontario thousands of dollars to provide for these people, who are homeless and friendless and quite incapable of earning a living in this country. More precautions are needed. ' Quality, not quantity/ should be a rule from which there should be no deviation. More than ever before Ontario has been made, during the past year, the dumping ground of a most undesirable class. Charity may suffer long and be kind, but this province cannot afford to permit the bonused and designing agent abroad to continue as he has been doing during the past year, and the manner in which some of our charities have been imposed upon fully justifies this protest.
This is true also of my own province. Then I find that on March 18. before the Irish Protestant Benevolent Society's banquet at Toronto, Lieutenant Governor Clark said this:
Our province is in a crucial stage at present. Influx of new population, of people who have had strange ideas about liberty and religion, is endangering our state. These people come here believing that liberty means license and as such are a menace to our institutions.
A class of people come here who call themselves English or Irish or Scotch. True, they are British born, but they are not British at heart. They are children of foreign parents, who came to the British Islands years before. The babies were born in the British Islands, but they were partakers of foreign dispositions. They are not bred to principles we know of and might at the ballot-box seriously injure us.
It is a most serious question with which we must grapple. The United States, our neighbours to the south, have had, no doubt, the same troubles, and have to some extent assimilated this objectionable element in their population. But you must have noticed how crime is on the increase in Canada-crime of an abominable character. Evil deeds are rife in this land which we never knew before. Our nation was a better one before these people came. I am glad, and we should all be glad, that our questions of state and our institutions have been so largely settled before these people came.
I find here a resolution .which is rather long, and I will not trouble' the House with reading it, exactly in the same sense, passed by the Associated Charities of Toronto. This condition of affairs in Toronto is exactly repeated in the province of Quebec. I see that the eminent authority I have just quoted speaks of the possibility of assimilation. Now in this connection let me say this : The population of the United States numbered
50.000.	000 souls before immigration into that country reached 300,000 per annum. We have in this country about 6,000,000, and we received last year over 250,000 immigrants. Now to meet the proportion between the number of immigrants that came this year into the United States and its present population of SO,000,000, we would have to have
20.000.	000. Those who visit the United States, men of the very highest authority in sociology, like Mr. H. J. Weis, Viscount D'Avenel

who lias a European reputation, and Mr. Doumer, a French publicist, all agree that this immigration constitutes a grave peril to the United States. President Roosevelt himself said that this immigration is leading the nation to disaster. This year he has named, as I have already said, a commission of nine of the ablest experts to visit Europe and see what can be done to check the outflow of immigration to the United States. Other writers I have quoted say, and have made calculations to show, that in twenty-five years, at the present rate of immigration, we will have a population of 30,000,000, not 10,000,000 of which will be Canadian born. Now under these circumstances how can one explain the indifference that has existed in Canada up to at least the last six months, with regard to the immigration policy of this government ? I think it is difficult to explain. If these figures are correct, we will find ourselves in a few years in this position, that the destinies of this country, its march towards the future, will be decided, not by ourselves who are the descendants of those who have settled the country and have built it up, but it will be settled by an alien population who have invaded the country.
One word now in connection with the care we must take respecting immigrants. During the past year we have had a large influx of Italian immigrants, many of whom have settled down in our cities. The question of the influence of this tide upon labour I will leave to others to treat, because the labour element is well represented in this House. As a matter of fact, in my own constituency, I know a large industry which has during the last year dismissed a great many Canadian employees and replaced them by Italians, because they work cheaper, and can live on wages that Canadians cannot live on. We all know how these Italian labourers live. They live in masses, they are able to work at much lower wages than our own people can live on, and consequently they become very dangerous competitors to our own labouring men. I find that during the year ending June 30, 1907, we had 12,771 Italian immigrants admitted into Canada. 'Were any of them bonused? I do not know. Certain it is that under our present system it is possible they were bonused. I do not see any difficulty in Italians reaching certain European countries which are under the bonus system, and getting tickets from the agent to come to Canada, and in one way or another the agent gets the bonus. I see no obstacle to that, and I would be glad to hear the Minister of the Interior declare that it is impossible, or tell ns how they get here. But that class is not a dangerous class. I have lived in Montreal, and I know the Italians. There are excellent Italians, and there are some that are not so desirable. Let me quote to the House a high Italian authority who is thus Mr. MONK.
reported in the Montreal ' Star ' of February 28, with regard to Italian immigration :
I know for a fact that over sixty per cent of the Italians that come to this country are convicted criminals. When a man gets into trouble in Italy and is convicted, he generally leaves the country after having served his sentence, as he finds that he is not wanted at home. For years Canada has been the dumping ground of these criminals. It used to be the United States, but. owing to the enforcement of stricter laws the United States are not so popular with my countrymen as they used to be. Canada is now their goal because it is so easy of access. No questions are asked, no certificates are necessary. If you are in good health you can land in Canada without any money, regardless of the fact that you may be a hardened criminal.
And believe me, the majority of the Italians do not come out here without good reason. Their own country has grown too warm for them and Canada offers ample shelter. If the Canadian government knew its business it would have immigration agents in Italy whose duty it would be to inquire into the characters of intending emigrants.
The American authorities have done that.
Until some action of this kind is taken, the trouble that the respectable citizens of the city and the Dominion are now suffering from will never be eradicated. Almost without1 exception the men Italians found carrying^ arms are criminals and ex-convicts, who don't feel safe without a gun or stiletto. They come out here because they are too well known in their own country. Their actions here cast discredit upon the land of their birth.
I have no doubt that everybody here labours under the impression that in Italy every man goes about armed and that murders and stabbing cases are of hourly occurrence. Let me tell you that this is far from being the case. When a man is found carrying concealed weapons in Italy he does not get the chance of paying a fine. Instead he gets a long term of imprisonment. They don't believe, in fines for that sort of thing over there. But as a matter of fact the people there are not in the habit of going about armed with revolvers and razors and such like things. Thev are for the most part respectable, law-abiding citizens, who are particularly fortunate in that their criminals leave them in peace and emigrate to Canada, or some other country.
Murders are no more frequent in Italy than in any other country. There is more crime committed in Montreal in a week
I presume he is speaking of last winter :

city. The Italians here-I mean the most of them-are desperate men and the law will require to be strengthened in order to deal with them.

This is rather a long agreement, but it is a hard and fast agreement and one which places the immigrant almost entirely in tin; power of this Mr. Smart. But, let us look at how it turns out. The advance for the cost of transportation is the moderate amount of $55 for the man and his family to the point where he is to be employed. He will pay $4.50 a week for board to (lie Grand Trunk Pacific or any other company for six months which will make $120. For medical attendance he will pay $6. That is the payment, I have been informed, that is generally made. Deed of contract is $5 and the incidentals mentioned in the contract will amount to $15. All these are extremely moderate charges and they would very easily be increased. These make a total of $201 to his debit. Give him six months or about 125 days at $2 a day and he earns $250. After deducting his expenses he has at the end of six months $49 to himself. Is it surprising that these men are wandering back to the large cities and becoming a charge on the community ?
One word as regards these societies which of late have entered, particularly in England, into the field of immigration. For my part I state frankly that I would have more confidence in these societies even en-

tering the flelcl of immigration than I would have in the booking agents to whom I have already referred, from all the information I have regarding the natural and easily understood inclination and interest of the booking agents. The Salvation Army, in particular, does excellent work. I am speaking generally and outside of that phase of its work which has to do with immigration. It has done an immense amount of good in England and it is doing a great deal of good in this country. I am always happy if I can assist this work, because, as was very properly said by Cardinal Manning, speaking in London, the Salvation Army reaches a class of unfortunates that no other organized religion can possibly reach. That is true and it is doing a great deal of good, but still, when you consider it as entering the field of immigration and receiving a bonus you are obliged to consider the classes among which it works. Many of this class are reclaimed, are redeemed and many, I have no doubt, make good immigrants. We are dealing with conscientious men when we are dealing with the soldiers of the Salvation Army, the Church Army, the East End Church Army and these religious organizations. But let us be perfectly frank and say that the immigrants they recruit- not all, but a good many-are recruited among people who are dependent in England uppn public charity. They are men who have not succeeded in life, who have been assistant painters or assistant plumbers, who have not been able to succeed in their trades, who have large families, who are on the poor rates and it has been the habit of the guardians of the poor to confide a large number of these people to the Salvation Army, giving them a certain amount to take charge of these poor people, and they have all the necessary machinery to ship them to Canada. These are not in all cases the immigrants who are desired and I think it would be necessary for us, before paying bonuses in such cases, if we are to continue the bonusing system at all, to exercise the very greatest surveillance and to see that the unfortunate classes among whom these organizations work are not the classes that are sent out here.
There is an impression in England that all these undesirable people may be safely sent out here because they believe this to be a land flowing with milk and honey where there is always something to do even for the least qualified. It is the same in Calabria and the Neapolitan districts whence the most dangerous class of immigrants come, they find it cheaper to pay for the transportation of these dangerous and criminal classes from Naples to America than to keep them in jail, and that is why so many of these sinister malefactors from Italy land in Canada. Therefore, with regard to the immigration by religious societies we cannot be too careful. Many Mr. MONK.
of these undesirable people, as was stated by the Italian whom I have quoted come from the United States. Indeed we should be very careful in granting bonuses on immigrants wrho come from the United States and who are not of that excellent farming class in the western states who settle on our cheaper and better land. The immigrants who come from the New England States, particularly the aliens, are dangerous. In support of that view I quote a letter received in Montreal by a friend of mine, from a very reliable authority, who says:
An estimate based on information from several sources places the number of unemployed men in this city (New York) at 40 per cent of the total; the wages of many still employed are being reduced. The employment bureaus are crowded as they have not been for years. The savings banks are being drawn upon heavily. The beneficial and insurance societies are feeling the effects of the times by lapsed membership and heavy borrowings on policies. Public charities are besieged for help. Our city magistrates states that their courts and prisons are crowded with men who have committeed no crime, but who have come to the extremity of their resources.
In view of such conditions in the United States I would warn the government that next summer we may expect a large influx of such people to Canada, and we cannot be too careful. I stated this afternoon that such had been the prosperity attendant on the operation of that mysterious Northern Atlantic Trading Company, the names of whose directors the Prime Minister was careful not to divulge on account of the danger of their committing suicide-that company made a great deal of money, and following their example, a great many other such combinations have been formed for the purpose of reaping profit out of this bonus system. In the city of Montreal we have a society called ' Ua Society de placement et d'immigration,' which is composed, if I am well informed, of many influential members of the Liberal party who expect to get a bonus on immigrants from France. They have received a bonus of $2,090 from the provincial government, and the Minister of the Interior will correct me if I am wrong when I say, they have received or are going to receive, $5,000 from the Dominion government. I was told in reply to a question put by me in the House the other day, that they had not yet received any money, but my information is that they are to receive $5,000 from the Dominion government. Judging by their advertisement they have made arrangements to bring out farm hands and domestic servants. They will get a bonus from those with whom they make arrangements to bring out these people, and furthermore they are entitled to the large bonus which is paid on English immigrants. I think there is a danger in this. Societies of this kind are started

without any capital and they rely on the bonus for their income and for tlieir profit, and I think there is a danger in that. The truth is that we can obtain excellent immigrants from France, but in regard to France as well as in regard to every other country we should apply the rule that we must select the immigrants and be careful in the selection. Last year 17,000 French emigration from the Basque provinces went to the Argentine Republic. They are excellent settlers, and they left France from Bordeaux, Acachon and surrounding ports. But when immigrants get to the Argentine Republic they want to know who they are and they exact a certificate from each one of them, and in France every man carries a livret which gives his full record and which states whether he is really a farm hand, what lias been his business, what reputation he enjoyed in his own country* what is his record. We should impose a condition on all immigrants coming to Canada that they should have their livret which would show us their record.
Now, there is another matter to which I wish to call the attention of the government. Sometimes on these steamers from continental European ports there are as many as 2,000 immigrants and taking into account the crew and other passengers there sometimes are 2,400 persons on one of these steamers which will carry only perhaps 30 boats. That of course, would be impossible from a British port, but in the case of a vessel sailing from a continental European port the number of life boats is inadequate to save the passengers should the vessel meet with an accident which would necessitate those on board taking to the boats. I would suggest to the Minister of Marine and Fisheries that he should take this matter into his consideration, for should any frightful loss of life occur under such circumstances the government would be held responsible because of its failure to provide safeguarding legislation.
Now, Sir, as a practical conclusion I would say this: We should first nnd foremost have the examination of immigrants conducted on the other side before they leave for Canada. This is done largely by the United States authorities and we should follow the example. When a man and his family arrive here it is very difficult to deport the mother or the father or some of the children nnd let the others remain here. Very often a family of immigrants has sold all their belongings in the country whence they came, and it might be cruel to deport them except in very extreme cases indeed. We are the masters as to whom we shall admit to Canada, and it ought be possible for us to provide on the other side for an examination into the physical, mental, and moral condition of tne immigrants, and to admit nobody into the Canadian family who is not thought fit to form part of it. The bonus system should be abolished altogther.
I think I have stated enough with regard to the bonus to show that it is time there should be an end put to that antiquated form of encouraging immigration. I venture to predict that if it is abolished we will receive the same number of immigrants, and we will most assuredly get a better class. But if we must have a bonus system I submit to the consideration of the House and the government that we should give the bonus to the immigrants themselves. Once we have found a man courageous enough to come with his family to this country, to give up his home in the old country, to settle down here and become a respectable and a valuable citizen, why not give the bonus to that man so that it may help him on his new career in this country. Under these circumstances, if we are to give some encouragement we could not give it in any better shape than a payment to the immigrant himself. I know my own opinions on the question of immigration are advanced. My own belief is that before long we will be obliged to adopt sterner measures, we will have to adopt the head tax. We know that in the United States they began with a head tax of $1, then they raised that by degrees to $4, and unquestionably they will still further increase the head tax in the United States. If we had a reasonable head tax we would immediately cover all this vast expense of over $1,000,000, we would secure better immigrants and we would receive as many as we are now receiving. Strange as it may appear, I am sure that if we had a head tax we would not diminish the number of immigrants. It has not diminished it in the United States. We would cover the whole $1,000,000 by means of the head tax and would provide a perfect system of inspection so that the immigrants would be in better shape than they are at present, and the $1,000,000 which is absolutely lost to us under the present conditions, could be devoted to more useful purposes.
I feel that in talking to the Minister of the Interior, who is charged more particularly with the Department of Immigration, I am, in a sense, speaking to a convert. My hon. friend the Minister of the Interior when he was an ordinary member of this House, gave to the House the benefit of his experience as a long resident in the North west. He has expressed to this House in far stronger and more eloquent words than I could, exactly the opinions which I expressed this afternoon. Time and again I have heard my hon, friend before he reached the high position which he occupies today, explain and uphold the views I have expressed. I shall not quote at length, because he never varied in his opinions until the change which took him from the seat lie occupied then, which was the seat of sincerity and truthfulness, to the ministerial position in which his views underwent, I

regret to say, a very serious change. Xu 3899 the minister among other things said at page 8523 of ' Hansard ' :
It is said: Look at the example of the United States. There is a country which has grown great by reason of opening its doors wide to the world. Well, let us see. The United States had a population of over 30,000,000 before the general influx of European population began. We, in Canada, have a population of possibly
5,000,000. There was no possibility of the original population of the United States being overwhelmed by the influx of foreigners from Europe. But there is every possibility of the population of northwestern Canada being overwhelmed. We must not forget the difference in out situations; and we must not forget that, after an experience of many years of the open door to the world-wide immigration, the United States years ago saw their mistake, and to a very great extent, shut the door. Now, if the example of the United States was good at one time, why is it not good now? Surely, the more mature judgment of the United States is as valuable to us as the less mature. If a nation of sixty or seventy millions finds it necessary to shut the door to indiscriminate [DOT] immigration, is it not more necessary for a country of five millions, especially when the part of the country affected, in which these eople will have almost sovereign powers, num-ers only half a million, or scarcely that.
Elsewhere my lion, friend said :
I give you the actual facts which speak for themselves. People have left their places because the Galicians came in and settled near them. These other people are the pioneers and not the Galicians. The latter came in and had the advantage of the experience of the others, and they settled in places which would be considered desirable for settlement by other people were it not for the fact that these Galicians came there. It is not necessary that they should occupy every quarter-section in order to keep other people out, because they have taken up a tract of country about 25 miles in length and there no other settlers will go, although the Galicians have not occupied every other quarter-section. On the face of it, it is plain that- this is a very serious question. While we have not suffered any very serious loss so far, I would not be doing justice to the district I represent were I not to place before this House and government the fact that there is danger, very serious, to the settlement of the Northwest, and particularly that part of the country, from the influence of thesa Galicians.
Further on he said :
You ask where are we to get people to fill up the Northwest? I looked over the United States census a few minutes ago and I found that in 1896 there were in the United States 980,938 natives born Canadians. Of these 678,442 were English and 302,496 French. There were of Canadian descent in the United States at that time 1,700,943 people. If it is true that there were in 1890 about 1,000,000 native born Canadians in the United States, if my calculation is good for anything, it means that there has been an overflow of population from Canada to the United States of not less than 30,000 people a year for 30 years. Where, then, can we find a better field for immigration to Mr. MONK.
the Noi'thwest than right in Canada itself, right in the older provinces? I know that that was contrary to the policy of the late government, as it is the policy of the present government, but is it not worth trying to get some of that 30,000 a year to go to the Northwest?
I cordially endorse, Mr. Speaker, these and many other statements made at that time by my hon. friend when he was completely' independent. Let ns reflect for a moment that the Doukhobors about whom we have heard a great deal lately, cost us to bring out here according to an answer given to a question in this House about $7.07 each. We expended over $40,000 at that time and they have cost us a great deal since then by reason of their being undesirable. Would not this House agree that the sum of $100,000 almost that we have spent on this class of people, clearly not the best, clearly not what we want in this country, could have been far better spent in the repatriation of this million and more of our fellow citizens in the United States, many of whom are anxious to get back to Canada, many of whom have never taken the oath of allegiance to the United States ? There is a valuable asset lying ready to return to this country and could we not better have spent all our money on these people, than on adding an undesirable element to our population? The Minister of the Interior expressed these and far stronger views at the time. I have only given, the House a sample of them. How changed he is today. What is it that has brought about this change? The contact with the gentlemen whom he met when he entered the cabinet ? When he was a private member of this House the Minister of the Interior was the knight errant of what I would call the noble and proper principle for Canadian immigration ; but bold knights vanish very quickly under such influences as seem to have been brought to bear on him since he entered the cabinet.
I feel confident that the time has arrived when we must not only look most carefully ihto this subject but must study the whole subject of immigration, and I venture to say that our whole system will have to be completely remodelled. We are a young country, we are at present the cynosure of the eyes of all Europe and the world generally. Canada is an immense country, a young country, full of resources, and the trend of the tide of immigration from all over the world is towards these shores. This is the hour for us to bring to bear all necessary precautions, a certain pride, a certain prudence, which should be our characteristic as a young nation ; we should see that only the very best elements enter this country and we, the older men, the descendants of those who were the pioneers of this country, who settled it, should make it our principal solicitude to have in Canada only those who are fit to be associated
with us in the grand work of building up here a great commonwealth.

speakeroldname: Hon. FRANK OLIVIER (Minister of the interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
subtopic: STATEMENT SHOWING WHAT PROPORTION OF OUR IMMIGRANTS GO UPON THE FREE LANDS OF THE NORTHWEST.
speechtext:
With a great deal of what my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) has placed before the House I can most cordially and heartily agree. He has not said one word too much with regard to the importance of immigration and its character. iBut I am sorry that he has moved a resolution in amendment to the motion to go into Supply in the terms lie did and that in supporting that motion he took the ground and made the speech he did. He . declares in his resolution that an aggressive immigration policy is desirable, but in his speech declares that the methods by which our immigration policy has been made successful are undesirable. My bon. friend is in the position of a successful business man who has achieved success by following certain methods and who then having achieved success decides to discard the methods which brought about that success. He admits that we have been successful in our immigration efforts, but regarding one very important part of that effort the bonusing of booking1 agents he has everything lie could to disparage it. While admitting that our immigration policy has been successful he has said everything he could to disparage every effort put forth by the government to encourage immigration and has been particularly desirous of discrediting this particular form of effort 1 cannot follow him-and I do not think that that would be desirable or in the interests of debate-in all the positions he has taken.
In the beginning of his remarks he spoke of Canada ns a country of five and a half million people with a very large territory to develop and very great opportunities and responsibilities. He then spoke of the United States a country of 80,0000 people, and of the splendid development which lias there taken place. And he undertook to draw a parallel with regard to immigration policies between the two countries. He undertook to show that because a certain line of action was particularly desirable in the United States, a country of 80000,000, that same line of action was equally desirable in Canada, a country of five and a half million people, but with an area equal to that of the United States. I have only to state the position to show how absurd bis contention is. My bon. friend did not remind the House that 125 years ago, at the time the United States became an independent country, it had about the population which the Dominion of Canada has to-day. The United States has been 125 years from that date arriving at the position it now occupies. Yet my hon. friend undertakes to say that the policy of Canada should be the same as that of the United states after 125 years successful effort. Ikat is sufficient to show how unwarranted were my bon. friend's comparisons. I do
not wish to make any reflections upon his remarks; but I notice that although no one in this House has greater ability in expressing himself correctly and concisely and in transferring his thoughts to the pages of ' Hansard ' without special assistance, he was careful to-day not to trust to his memory or the inspiration of the moment, but to- read carefully his matured conclusions with regard to this important subject. I assume that the importance of the question was part of the warrant for this unnecessary and unusual caution on his part. I assume that another reason was the importance of the position he occupies on this subject. I take it for granted that he voices the opinion of his party on this question, that his leader left this charge upon him when he left the House, and I have every confidence that he discharged his duty as well as his leader could have done or perhaps better. But it seemed to me that there was something more than all this in the necessity for the special care he took in the expressions that were to be used. It seemed to me that my hon. friend had one eye on the effect of his remarks upon those who are particularly interested against an overplus of labour in this country, while he had another eye just as wide open to the possible effect of his remarks on the financial manufacturing and transportation interests of this country. He was evidently travelling on a very narrow road and it was necessary he should not step off it on either side. Every one will admit that if immigration is a good thing, if it is a necessity for this country in its present condition-and T have my hon. friend's word that it is-it must be upheld by methods of business of one kind or another. Something must be done if the good result aimed at is to be achieved ; and when my hon. friend had been at such pains, as he was to-day, to discredit this important feature of the government's immigration policy and as far as he could, discredit all its methods, he must be satisfied to rank himself and his party against the principle of immigration to this country or against the principle of active effort on behalf of immigration. If that is tile position of my hon. friend and his policy, we are very glad to take issue with him. We believe that in a country of the limited population and the vast area 6f Canada to-day, immigration is necessary to its progress, prosperity and general well-being. We believe that a great part of the,prosperity and success which Canada enjoys to-day is due to the success of its immigration policy. My hon. friend read a great many figures which have more or less bearing on the question at issue, but he did not make what I think would have been a very illuminating statement. That would be a parallel between the flow of immigration and the increase of trade and general prosperity in Canada. He will find that the flow of immigration and the increase in the

volume of trade and general prosperity of the country absolutely inarch together from year to year.
My hon. friend has heard, or knows, that there are people out of employment in Canada-they were out of employment during the past winter. Did he ever hear, or does he remember, whether there were people out of employment in 1896 or the years preceding? He has heard of crime in Canada within the last few months. Was Canada free from crime previous to 1896? Is it a fact that there are fewer people out of employment than there were in 1896? It is a fact and my hon. friend knows that it is a fact. Notwithstanding the vast flow of immigration in the years between, notwithstanding the sudden change in financial conditions, only a few months ago, it is a fact to-day, that there are a less number of people out of employment in this Dominion of Canada than there were eleven years ago. That means, and can only mean, that Canada needed the people who came in the intervening years-that Canada needed these people, that these people have found a place in the well-being of Canada and that we have had the benefit of their coming. My hon. friend was eloquent on the desirability of keeping Canada for the Canadians, for those of us who were born here. Well, we want Canada for ourselves. But we cannot have something and at the same time give it away; we cannot keep Canada for ourselves without keeping it to work in for ourselves. If we are going to have other people In this country to help to develop the country and make money for us, we have to give them their share in the country. We could keep Canada for ourselves-our hon. friends opposite kept Canada for us very well, they were most successful in that policy. But I do not believe that even they themselves were satisfied with it; at any rate, the country was not. If we are to have that success in the development of the country that we look forward to, that we expect, that we plan for and work for, we can only have it by an increase in the number of workers in the country; and we can get that increase in the number of workers by bringing people from other countries to help us develop this country.
In regard to this particular question of bonus, I think it is just as well that we should deal with that matter at some length. I am glad my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) dealt with it, because I believe there is a very widespread wrong impression in regard to it. And, just in passing, I must thank my hon. friend for having read to this House the remarks which I made some years ago. I would like to say to him that what I said then seemed to me just as good as it seemed to him, and it seems to me just as good to-day as it did then, and expresses my opinion and my policy-so far as I may speak of my policy-to-day, as it did then. I will not remind the House, however, that Mr. OLIVER.
when I gave expression to-these views, I had not a solitary endorser on that side of the House.

I do not know what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sam. Hughes) is alluding to, and I do not know whether he knows himself or not. I repeat that the views I expressed in regard to indiscriminate immigration I hold to-day as strongly as I held then. The policy of the government to-day is to carry out these views-let there be no mistake on that point. And the system of bonuses, as it is at present administered, is distinctly a system of selected immigration -so intended, so carried out, and successful in being carried out. Because bonuses are given, it does not follow that they are an inducement to indiscriminate immigration. Advertising may be necessary in carrying on a certain business, but the advertising may be one kind or it mcly be of another kind. Your canvasser may put forward one kind of argument or he may put forward another. So the system of offering bonuses may be put forward in one way or it may be put forward in another way. And to-day the matter does not admit of question that the system of bonuses as now administered is distinctly and specially a system looking toward selected, not toward indiscriminate, immigration.
My hon. friend was very much perturbed about the possibility of our paying bonuses on people, who, having come to Canada, pass on to the United States. He did not know how we avoid paying these bonuses, or how, if we paid them, we could possibly get the'money back. I am afraid he did not study his own remarks before he made them as well as he should have done. He told the House that the United States keeps a most careful check upon all immigrants passing from Canada into the United States. He told the House what this check at the hands of the United States government rereveal to him, He had every faith that it was a complete check, that it w-as absolute and correct. He must know that, if this information was abialable to him, it is just as available to the officers of the Canadian Immigration Department, and that, by co-operation with the officials of the United States immigration service, it is possible for us to have the same advantage of an absolute check upon the immigrants passing through Canada to the United States-check in which the hon. gentleman reposes the most implicit confidence. Therefore, we do know, as a matter of fact, from the returns of the United States government, exactly how many, and exactly

who, of the immigrants who have come to Canada have passed to the United States ; and if, upon any of these, bonus has been paid, that amount is deducted from the next amount due that booking agent on bonus account. Nothing could be simpler, nothing could be easier, and nothing could be more satisfactory it seems to me.

speechtext:
My hon. friend will agree with me that there are more things in heaven and earth than are covered by the reports made to this House. It seems to me that the reports made to the House, not excluding the numerous returns asked for from time to time, receive very little attention from the House or country, judging from the discussions that take place on this floor. However, if this has not been reported before, I hope the hon. gentleman will consider that it has been reported now, and that he is aware how this payment of bonus is checked by the Canadian Immigration Department.
My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) enlarged greatly upon the enormous amount that had been paid in bonuses, aud the stupendous danger of paying money upon undesirables. He spoke of our receiving 100,000 immigrants from European countries and suggested to the House, so that it might be reported to the country, that there was a probability, a reasonable probability, that bonus had been paid on every one of these immigrants. Now, he knew perfectly well that there was no foundation for that statement-pardon me, I should not say that; but the figures in his hand which he read to the House showed that there was no foundation for the statement. Just to recall some of those figures, he gave the House something like this: From the United States there was an immigration in a certain year of 30,000 of
40,000	people, and on that immigration there was some $3,000 paid in bonuses. In regard to general immigration there was in 1904-5, 146,266 immigrants arriving, and bonuses were paid on 28,836, or a little less than one in five of all those that arrived in that year. In 1905-6, 189,000 arrived, and a bonus was paid on 33,608. In 1906-7, nine months, 124,667 arrived, and a bonus was paid on 14,094; that is about one in nine. In 1907-8, nine months, 235,328 immigrants arrived and a bonus was paid on 20,492, that is about one in twelve.
