speechtext: I have given my hon. friend four years ; so while it is quite true that some accounts are yet unsettled, I think they will balance each other. At any rate, we are not paying on a greater proportion of the total arrivals than I have just indicated. Now what do these figures 213

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.

speechtext:
show ? They show first that we are not paying a bonus on all immigrants who arrive ; they show that the number on which we are paying is from one in five to one in twelve of all those who arrive. That shows that our officers are exercising due diligence in carrying out our regulations and that they are exercising proper care in the payment of bonuses that my hon. friend was very careful not to give them credit for in his remarks. He gave the idea to the House that there was collusion between the officers of the department and these immigration companies. If there was collusion, certainly the moderation of these people is wonderful. If there is an improper agreement between these companies and the officers of the government, and if having that free hand my hon. friend has suggested, they only paid bonuses on one in five or one in twelve that came over, certainly they are a very moderate minded people. But in point of fact, the hon. gentleman's figures disprove his contention ; they prove absolutely that the regulations regarding the payment of bonuses are effective, and that they are honestly administered. Now, if they are effective and honestly administered, and if the bonus figures are as I have just stated them, the conclusion is irresistible that the bonuses are paid with discrimination, and are not paid indiscriminately. If we pay on only one in five, or one in ten, or one in twelve, we must pay on that small percentage for some reason, there must be some basis on which we make the payment. Now why did we pay on that small number ? Because they are the classes of people that are satisfactory to us, the kind of people that my hon. friend himself will not dare to say should not be admitted to this country, or should not even be encouraged to come here. The figures I repeat are proof absolute that the policy of the government is a policy of discrimination in regard to immigration, and that the payment of bonuses made in pursuance of that policy is effective in carrying out the policy.
My hon. friend was worried about the North Atlantic Trading Company, and he thought the North Atlantic Trading Company had numerous successors who, I suppose, he wished us to understand were even worse than the North Atlantic Trading Company, more secretive and| more ravenous. He knows that the agreement with the North Atlantic Trading Company was terminated on the 30th of November,
1906.	From that time forward no bonuses were paid on continental immigrants until the order in council that was passed in
1907,	and then a bonus of ten shillings was paid on adults to selected booking agents in certain European countries. Under that system, during the months from March. 1907, to February, 1908, bonus was paid to these selected booking agents for immi-

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.

speechtext:
grunts of the classes described coming from certain countries of Europe, to the number of 1,211 men, 390 women, 555 children, or £930 in all. That is all the bonuses paid on continental immigrants under the system which the hon. gentleman has been pleased to term a system of indiscriminate bonusing of immigrants coming from the continent of Europe. He has been good enough to say that in all probability the bonus has been paid on Italians, and he seems to have a very strong objection to such a thing. Now for good or bad reasons the government has not paid any bonuses on people coming from Italy since some time I think in 1902. Italy was one of the countries where a bonus was paid on immigrants to the North Atlantic Trading Company, I think in the first year of its operation. But the bonus was withdrawn as regards Italy and several other southern European countries, and since then no bonus has been paid on immigrants from Italy. The total number of immigrants coming from Italy on whom bonuses were paid, were I think in all 72, and that was five or six years ago. So that whatever may be charged against the bonus system, certainly the objections which my hon. friend has expressed to the Italian residents of this country are not chargeable to that system. In order to make it perfectly plain that the policy of the government is one of discrimination, it is only necessary to read the provisions of the immigration law, to which my hon. friend gave his assent in the session of 1906. Let me remind him and others of my hon. friends on the other side that their assent was not by any means a cordial assent to the provisions of the Act. They had a great deal of fault to find with a good many of its provisions, nearly as much fault as they have to find with the provisions of the regulations regarding bonuses. But, remember that Act was passed and it is in force and it is being enforced. Nothing can be plainer than the intent of the government and of parliament at that time was that while there should be an active and energetic effort made to secure a good and desirable class of immigrants for this country' it should be a part of that policy, a very necessary part of it, that there should be accompanying these aggressive measures to bring immigrants, parallel energetic and effective measures to exclude undesirable immigrants. That was the mandate of parliament expressed in the session of 1906, embodied in the provisions of the Immigration Act and has been the policy that the government has carried out ever since. My hon. friend has been pathetic as to the woes of the municipalities, especially in Ontario and Quebec brought about by reason of the presence of undesirable immigrants. The city of Montreal, it seems, has been plagued with them, and the city of To-Mr. OLIVER.
ronto has been plagued with them. I do not know but that a great many other places may have been plagued with them. I notice that the city of Montreal is very glad to publish from time to time the statement, blazoned as largely as possible, that the population of Montreal has increased over a previous period and that the city of Toronto is doing likewise. These municipalities are glad to announce that their population has increased, but you cannot have an increase of population without having an increase of people and if you have an increase of people you can hardly have it without having an increase of the disabilities and disadvantages that go with ordinary people in this country. If the city of Montreal, or the city of Toronto, or any other municipality has suffered in the way my hon. friend has said then it is the fault of Montreal, the fault of Toronto, the fault of the other municipality and not the fault of this government or of its Act or its administration. Section 32 of the Immigration law says :
All railway or transportation companies or other persons bringing immigrants from any country into Canada shall, on the demand of the Superintendent of Immigration, deport to the country whence he was brought, any immigrant prohibited by this Act, or bv any order in council or regulation made thereunder, from being landed in Canada, who was brought by such railway, transportation company or other person into Canada within a period of two years prior to the date of such demand.
Section 33 says :
Whenever in Canada an immigrant has, within two years of his landing in Canada, committed a crime involving moral turpitude, or become an inmate of a gaol or hospital or other charitable institution, it shall be the duty of the clerk or secretary of the municipality to forthwith notify the minister thereof, giving full particulars.
2. On receipt of such information the minister may, on investigating the facts, order the deportation of such immigrant at the cost and charges of such immigrant if he is able to pay, and if not then at the cost of the municipality wherein he has last been regularly resident, if so ordered by the minister, and if he is a vagrant or tramp, or there is no such municipality, then at the cost of the Department of the Interior.
That is the law. That was the law passed by parliament. That is the law under which the government is working and I say that under the provisions of that law, if any municipality complains as my hon. friend says they complain, it has no ground to complain of the Immigration Department or of this Liberal government, because in every case, where representations were made by a municipality deportation has been carried out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Do I understand that deportation can take place at the cost of the municipality ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
Yes, but it can also be made at the cost of the government, but the point I wish to emphasise is that if a municipality wants an immigrant deported the provisions of the law are there and under these provisions he can be deported. If he is not deported it is not the flault of the law and it is not the fault of this government. I agree with what my hon. friend has said that it is a tremendous hardship to deport people. It is a must unfortunate thing when deportation has to be carried out. I quite appreciate the consideration of the municipalities in not asking for deportation of unfortunates who are within their limits. It is to the credit of the municipalities that they should have such a large feeling of charity, but there is the law and if they do not want to take advantage of its provisions I submit that they have no right to complain of the government which does not carry out the law except upon their demand, and especially there is no cause of complaint from our hon. friends opposite who are a party as much as we are to the provisions of this law. My. hon. friend also found fault with us because we allowed the people to get into the country that should be kept out. He said that the hurry and rush of landing passengers made it impossible to preserve an absolute check upon them on their arrival. Admitting the truth of that there is still the provision for the deportation of any undesirable who comes in. If he is discovered within two years he may be sent out. But in regard to the actual conduct of the examination at the port of landing, it is not the mere formal affair that the hon. gentleman suggests. It is true that a large number of people have to be landed in a very short time, but it is also true that on the slightest suspicion that anything is wrong with any of these people they may be taken aside from the general rush and held for examination. That is done and there is a very large number checked at the port of landing and returned from that port. He says that the provisions of the United States at these ports of landing are more efficient than ours. Possibly they are, but I would call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that to-day in the House and in the papers of this country there was blazoned abroad a complaint that the medical officer of the Immigration Department at the port of Halifax had delayed unduly a steamship load of immigrants. The same gentlemen who are demanding greater delay in the landing of immigrants, who are demanding that there shall be more particular examination, which means certainly either a very much greater expense to this country or a much greater delay to passengers, are complaining because they 2131
say that a load of passengers was unduly delayed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
The newspaper was careful not to say that he was not attending to his duties as he should, but it said there was a delay of the passengers and I submit that the hours mentioned did not show there was an undue delay, but quite the contrary. It shows that this statement was sent broadcast through the country just as a thousand other slanders have been sent broadcast through the country, and with just as little justification. The United States is at present pursuing a policy of exclusion of immigrants; it has no policy of bringing in immigrants. If we are to take the policy of the United States then we know exactly what to do and we can do as they are doing. I hope that if we ever have to undertake such a policy we will be more successful than they are, because, with their efforts at exclusion they received last year over one million immigrants and of that one million from 45 per cent to 50 per cent were of the very class which our friends on the other side of the House consider as being undesirable for Canada. The immigration situation in the United States differs materially from our situation. Their climatic and other conditions are attractive to a certain class of people that our country is not attractive to. Certain phases of the immigration question loom large to them where they loom small to us because of different conditions. Their attitude is one specially of exclusion but ours is not an attitude of exclusion. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) did not dare-I use the word without offence-did not dare to put upon the records of parliament a motion declaring for an exclusion policy; he did not dare to say that he was against a policy of active immigration. And as long as this country is to have a policy of attraction for immigrants it cannot handle its immigrants as they come at the ports of landing as would a country which has a distinctly exclusion policy. We must give facilities for our immigrants to land with the least possible discomfort. We must so conduct our business at the ports that we shall not exclude those whom we desire to

come here. In the United States they can exclude everybody, that is their law, that is their policy, that is their business. But it is not ours, and we cannot carry on our business at our ports ns they carry on their business at theirs. I am bound to say that after all, although we do not have nearly as large a staff at our ports as they have at theirs, although we do not take up nearly as much time as they do, in the last result we have just about as effective inspection of immigrants as they have. They have, by agreement with ' the Canadian government, an inspection of immigrants bound for the United States, at Halifax, Montreal, Quebec and St. John, where they handle their immigrants just the same as if they were landing at United States ports. My hon. friend (Mr. Monk) was terribly worried about what became of immigrants excluded at Canadian ports by United States officials. I can tell him what becomes of them. If a passenger ticketed for the United States is excluded by a United States official at a Canadian port he goes back on the steamship he came on. The same rule prevails at New York ; if an immigrant arrives at New York ticketed for Canada and if our officer there says he is to be excluded the United States authorities see that he goes back on the steamer he came on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Have we an examining officer at Ellis Island ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Yes.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Who is he ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Doctor Elliot.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: The minister said that the newspaper did not state that this doctor at Halifax was not charged with being absent from his post.	.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I said that the newspaper did not charge he was canvassing when he should be at his post.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I don't care whether he was canvassing or anything else, lie was not attending to his business, and I will read what the newspaper says if the minister will permit me.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I don't think that has anything to do with the question I am dealing with now.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: The newspaper says the doctor did not come there from early morning till three o'clock in the afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
We are inquiring into the matter, and I hope to be able to lay before the House a statement with regard to it. I can assure the House that if the doctor at Halifax was not attending to his duties when he should have been, we will probably be able to get along without his valuable services. This question of dealing with immigrants on their arrival is a serious question, it is a difficult question, it is an im-Mr OLIVER,
portant question. I beg to assure my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) that the government appreciates just as highly as he does the importance of excluding undesirables from this country and has taken all active measures that can be taken to achieve that end. But it is one thing to take the position that we are there simply for the purpose of excluding, and another thing to take the position that we are there principally for the purpose of bringing into our country those whom we desire to assist us in building our country up. That is the difficulty that confronts the Dominion government in dealing with this question of immigration, and we certainly think we are entitled to a fair consideration from our friends on the other side of the House in our efforts 'to deal wi|th that question, rather than that we should be met by what I consider to be unfair criticism of details of the policy in regard to difficulties which cannot be avoided and which are inseparable from the carrying out of the dual policy of aggressive immigration effort on the one hand and exclusion of undesirables on the other. That I take it is the policy of this government. Let there be no mistake about it. And, one part of it is just as important as the other. It is just as important that we should use our efforts and spend our money to bring desirable immigrants to Canada as it is that we should keep out undesirable immigrants. Our friends opposite have during several sessions assumed, and their press throughout the country has assumed, that the government's policy was a policy of indiscriminate immigration, and yet there was a law on the statute-book and there was enforcement of the law at every port. My hon. friends opposite have no warrant for the position they took, and if they had ever a warrant for that position they have no warrant from this time onward. It is not long ago since in an effort to make it possible to carry out our understanding and to compel the fulfilment of our obligations, there was before the House a little amendment to the Immigration Act; a trifling little matter of some four or five lines. It was an absolute necessity to the intelligent and effective enforcement of certain provisions of the law. We have to face an immigration question on the Pacific as well as on the Atlantic. It is different on the Pacific from what it is on the Atlantic. The immigration differs at every point of the compass. It was necessary to adopt a restrictive policy on the Pacific coast. Different measures were suggested in regard to that restrictive policy but it was thought well in the interest of the country, in the interest of the empire, that a conciliatory rather than an aggressive policy should be adopted in connection with the immigration from one country at any rate. In pursuance of that idea an amicable arrangement was arrived at with that country, and it is hoped that a

similar arrangement can be arrived at -with another country that is in a somewhat similar position in regard to immigration. _ But an agreement with Japan as to the .restriction of immigrants from Japan to~Canada, or an agreement with the government of India as to the restriction of immigrants from India to Canada was of no value without the provision we asked this House to pass the other night. It was absolutely of no effect.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Did the minister say that the regulations passed by the House were above the treaty ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: No I did not say anything about the treaty. The gentleman who should be my hon. friend's leader took occasion to state his opinion to the House on that subject, but I do not think he maintained it, I think he was very glad to drop it before he got very far. However, my hon. friend will have an opportunity to maintain that same position at a later stage of this debate. My statement was that the agreement we arrived at with Japan and the agreement we hoped to arrive at with the government of India, agreements which are' absolutely necessary in pursuance of our immigration policy and our trade policy on the Pacific coast, did not receive enthusiastic endorsation from our friends on the other side. I was surprised to see that. After the question had been threshed out for an hour, and the amendment had been twisted in every direction, when it was explained to our hon. friends that it was a matter of urgency to have this little amendment to the immigration law passed that evening, the Prime Minister was refused that courtesy, he was told it could not be passed, although our friends opposite had been informed that the date of its going into effect might be deferred for three or four weeks, and that as a consequence very serious complications might have arisen. I was glad to see when the House met the next day that our friends had experienced a change of heart ; there was nothing wrong with the little amendment to the Immigration Act and it went through without change.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I think the minister should be fair enough to admit that it was the amendment of my hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) that prevented it going through the first night. He was not here the next night and in his absence it went through ; that was the only cause of delay the first night.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) has a great deal to answer for on that side of the House, but I do not think he was entirely responsible in this case.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
Yes, I was wholly and entirely responsible for holding back
the Bill, and if it had been held back for ten minutes longer the next evening it would have been delayed still more.
Mr. OLIVER, I am not here to argue. I merely, state the facts. I instance this to show that the government's policy is well defined, that it is a continuous policy, and that it does not receive that support from our friends on the other side that their remarks from time to time would indicate it should receive at their hands. VVe have not only the provisions of this Immigration Act which I have already mentioned to the House, but have found it necessary on account of the changed conditions in this country during the last few months to make certain changes in the administration of the law such as we are empowered to make by the provisions of the Act ; because my friends will notice that while the Immigration Act contains certain very definite provisions, it also recognizes that new conditions may arise at any time and that it is necessary that the government should have the power to meet these new conditions as they arise. Provision is made in the Act for the passing of regulations by order in council to meet such conditions as may arise from time to time. Taking advantage of that provision in the Act, last fall when there was a change in the condition of the country that seemed to make it very desirable, we provided that there should be a money qualification in certain circumstances on the part of immigrants arriving in this country. That I hope my hon. friends will consider is not an indication of a policy of unrestricted immigration. On representations made by our agent in Great Britain, Mr. Bruce Walker who was then assistant superintendent of Immigration in London, in regard to the work of the charitable associations in Great Britain and its effect upon the immigration situation in Canada, we passed on the 25th of February another regulation which provided that persons coming to Canada by assisted passage could be excluded unless they were approved before they left their homes by our agent in that country. This is surely not an indication of a policy of unrestricted immigration. Surely these regulations bear out my statement that the avowed policy of this government is a policy of selected immigration, is a policy of restricted immigration if you like, while at the same time, it is a policy of aggressive immigration.
In order that there may be no mistake about the attitude the government assumes the government aware of its responsibilities, aware of the requirements of the country and carrying out its policy of selected immigration makes announcement in large type on the first page of its latest publications, the following :

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.

speechtext: Farmers, farm labourers, railway construction men and female domestic servants are

the only people the Canadian Immigration Department advise to emigrate to Canada. All others should get definite assurance of ern-loyment in Canada before leaving home and ave money enough to support them for a time in case of disappointment.
That is an expression of the immigration policy of the government of Canada to-day as set out in the printed representations they make to the people whom they desire to come to the country. How, in the face of that, can my hon. friend suggest that our policy is a policy of unrestricted or indiscriminate immigration ? We cannot be held responsible for the efforts of charitable associations. We cannot be held responsible for the movement, of free citizens of other countries who choose to come to this country. We can only be held responsible for the efforts we make, and we make those efforts only to secure the classes of people that I mention. No one in this House, even at this time, will suggest that this is not desirable, that it is not in the best interests of the Dominion of Canada that reasonable efforts should be made to induce these classes of people to come to this country.
What was the condition a year ago in Canada? At that time, from one end of Canada to the other, there was a demand for unskilled labour. The demand was loud and insistent from every part of the country. It was proclaimed in the newspapers that railway construction was being held back because there were not sufficient people to work on the railway; that the factories could not fill their orders because they could not get operatives; that the farmers could not work their land because they could not get the farm help they required. And at the same time the broad fields in the Northwest were waiting settlement. What policy, in such circumstances, could be suggested for a progressive government but a policy of aggressive immigration? It is not so very long since we had a session of parliament here. The intervals between sessions seem to be getting shorter as the country gets older. It is just about a year ago to-day, or a little over, that we had a discussion in this House on the question of immigration, and some of our friends opposite then relieved their minds on this question. At that time there seemed to have been a rather strong-sentiment in favour of immigration. My hon. friend from Montmagny (Mr. La-vergne) had some thing to say. I fancy he will follow the lead of my hon. friends on the other side and declare against immigration to-day. A year ago my hon. friend from Montmagny said:
There is another feature of the immigration policy of this government which I desire to call to the attention of this House and the country in general. It is the most unjust way i j which French immigration and the province cf Quebec has been treated.
Mr. OLIV FT?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I did not say that. The hon. gentleman is mistaken.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: He did not say It ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I did not mean it either.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: He did not say anything in the whole course of his remarks.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Why then this reference?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: In my opinion he did not say anything, but this is as near as he came to saying anything, and what I gather from it was that he was dissatisfied because the government had not used greater endeavours in order to secure more people for the province of Quebec.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: The hon. gentleman is again mistaken, but no doubt that is as near as he can come to understanding what I said.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
My hon. friend is absolutely correct. That is as near as I can claim to an understanding of his remarks. I submit them, as they appear in * Hansard ' to the House for special consideration. He said further :
I could also give figures to show that the French immigrant has cost less to this country than the British, and I only mention this to show that if the Department of the Interior were not so savagely opposed to it, it would be easy to bring French emigrants to this country.
We had an hon. member in this House at that time, who, we are pleased to see, is not among us now. I refer to the hon. member for Labelle.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
He discussed the question of immigration. He said:
My views are these. Because the fathers of confederation decided, and decided cvisely, that this should be a dual country-French in its origin, British by assimilation, taking from both races and both civilizations its best moral, social and political characteristics-I maintain that the equilibrium between the two should be maintained, and it is in the interests of all British citizens in Canada that Frenchspeaking population should be developed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: My hon. friend to-day is in favour of more immigration.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Hear, hear. The hon. gentleman ought to remember too that we favoured interior immigration from one province to another which the government opposed then and opposes still.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
I shall have something to say on that later on. Our friend from Labelle (Mr. Bourassa)-after a considerable amount of remarks which I think were as difficult to bring to a conclusion as the re-

marks of my liou. friend from Montmagny (Sir. Lavergue)-also said:
But I claim that you can get from Scotland from Ireland, from England, from Belgium, from the north end of France, from Brittany, from Auvergne, from Franche Comte a most desirable class of immigrants. You can get from these mountains a hardy race of men who would come to our eastern provinces and take up small farms because any of them have a small capital at their disposal of $1,000, $2,000, $5,000 and as much as $10,000, who will go into the older provinces as some of them have done without any inducement whatever from the government without any literature being distributed amongst them, having come of their own will because they happened to learn something about Canada. ... I claim that we have room for a large number-perhaps not for hundreds of thousands.
I think the House will admit that the then hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bou-rassa) was advocating an increase of French Immigration to Quebec, and my hon. friend from Montmagny will not say that that occasion was the only one, in the course of his parliamentary experience, on which, when my hon. friend from Labelle said * yes ' that my hon. friend from Montmagny did not say: ' Me too.'

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman want an answer ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
No, I am satisfied. But my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) also had something to say on that occasion. He was rather strongly in favour of immigration at that time. He did not have so many faults to find with the policy of the government. He said:
Let us look at the present situation in France, and let us ask what the Canadian government has done to induce French settlers to come to Canada. . . . Nothing has been done by the government to induce such people to settle in Canada. . .
There are at present in France perhaps, ten millions of people who would be prepared if, in the proper way, the advantages of this country were shown to them, to consider emi-giation to Canada, large numbers of whom would come to this country-eligible people who would make excellent settlers and would quickly become accustomed not only to our pclitical institutions but to our national life in every sense.
To-night he has found serious fault with this government because it has spread its efforts in regard to immigration to the extent of paying a bonus to booking agents on settlers coming from France, and because having offered that bonus and continued it for the year at ten shillings, they increased it to $5* per head at the beginning of this year. He has experienced a change of heart or else he would not have found fault with the government for using reasonable endeavours to secure a desirable class of immigrants from France to Canada.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Because you are not taking the proper means.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: My hon. friend said that we should not give bonuses to booking ageuts, but that we ought possibly to pay bonuses to the immigrants themselves. Well, that policy was adopted by his friends when they were in power and it was a failure. It was found not desirable and, was abandoned by them. This government has not seen fit to revive it. Such a policy would be the policy of assisted immigration, and assisted immigration is distinctly contrary to the immigration policy of this government. Let that be distinctly understood.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: You assisted a great deal too much I think.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Except In the case of the Icelanders, in which a bonus is paid the shipping company, thus reducing the fare to that extent-and no one will question the propriety of using reasonable endeavours to get Icelandic immigration-with that exception this government has not spent any money in assisting immigration or with regard to assisted immigration. And I want to impress on the House that we have taken the position that assisted immigration is not desirable as a rule. We have taken power to absolutely exclude it unless it is first approved by our own officers in the country from which it starts. That makes our position on the subject of assisted immigration perfectly and absolutely clear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: You assisted the Doukhobor -paid $50,000 for that purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: We did assist the Doukho-bors. I think that what was done in regard to these people was that some concession was made, the same that was made in the case of the Icelanders-the bonus was used as a part payment on the transportation. There was some exception made-I am not now clear exactly what it was-to the rule in the case of the Doukhobors. But, as I had occasion to say to the House a little while ago, when this question was up before, what was done in regard to the Doukhobors was not done in the dark, but in the full light of day, and, with one or two exceptions, on which I need not dwell, the action of the government received the absolute assent of this House and of the press and the people of Canada. I say it is too late in the day to call in question the policy of the government in regard to the Doukhobors.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I do not like to interrupt the hon. gentleman: but what does he say regarding a trachomatous immigrant who is kept for six months in the hospital?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
A trachoma patient is required to pay his own expenses in the hospital, and, if he does not pay, the steamship company must pay or he goes back-that is

all there is in regard to that. I want to make it perfectly clear that the hospital treatment of trachoma is at the cost of the immigrant or of the shipping company. The immigrant arrives suffering from a 'disease which renders him undersirable. But it is a curable disease. Under our law. he is liable to exclusion and to be sent back on the steamship, and unless the steamship company is willing to pay the charges necessary to bring about his cure, back he goes and that is all there is about it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
That is not the law.
facturers an this country are handicapped very much by shortness of female help, particularly the canners. I would like the minister to consider whether it would not be well to encourage women to come over, and give a bonus on bringing them as well as the men.
And another hon. gentleman on that side, whom I see in his place, said :
I will ask the government to make a more intelligent and more active propaganda in 1 ranee where we have but two agencies. I should think that our efforts should be directed especially towards securing emigrants in provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
Well, it is the practice. And if there is no law for it, I hope he will not be one to raise a question as to the system under which we are acting. It seems a reasonable and proper system and one that exactly meets the views he expresses. So far as the Pacific coast is concerned we have there, in view of our present attitude in regard to immigration, ceased to give treatment in these hospitals; so, when a trachoma patient arrives on the Pacific coast, he is sent back on the ship on which he came. Another hon. member of the House had something to say on the occasion of that debate ;
dliis shows that the policy of the Immigration Department is to direct these immigrants to the western lands

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. Oliver) say that they are not going to the United States yet?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I say there is not one of our native Canadian population going to the United States for ten that went fifteen years ago.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: The United States report of last year says that in 1907, there were 19,918 Canadians went to the United States.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: It is the same as ever-there is no change.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I can only say that my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) has more faith in the United States returns than I have. I think I can produce evidence that is better than any return. Previous to 1896, there was in some of the New England cities an absolute preponderance of French Canadians. At the same time there was not in the Canadian Northwest any appreciable increase of Canadian population. These facts are within the knowledge of every man in this House, and they do not need to be supported by reports of immigration officers or by census returns. That there are a million and more of Canadians in the States, any person who travels in the States will know. Go to any of the large cities in the United States and you will find a Canadian club ; go into any legislature of the western States and you will find Canadians occupying positions of more or less prominence. In every part of the United States are our people to be found. They went there instead of going to populate our own country, but to-day our country is being populated by our own people. We are getting people from other countries, it is true, but the most satisfactory feature about it is that our own people are going to our own Canadian Northwest, so that notwithstanding the inrush of people from Europe and the United States, to-day Canadians are the dominating influence through the four western provinces. That result has been achieved under the present immigration policy that my hon. friend deplores as one likely to de-Canadianize this country. It was the policy of hon. gentlemen opposite that de-Canadianized Canada, and that Canadian-ized every one of the northern States. This country cannot stand still, it must either go forward or backward. The immigration policy of this government is a policy of going forward ; the policy of my hon. friends whin they were in office was a policy of going backward. To-day the hon. gentleman. seeing a little change in the financial condition of the country, thinks he sees an opportunity to secure a party advantage at the expense of the country, and he proceeds to take it, and no doubt will have able assistance from hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. We have confidence in the intelligence of the Canadian people and their ability to understand the situation. We deny absolutely the accusation that the policy of this country is one of indiscriminate immigration. It is a policy of discriminating immigration, a policy that only looks to getting the best and excluding those that are not the best, so far as that is possible. On that line we are working and on the results achieved we desire to be judged.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: I think I can congratulate the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) in having deserved the compliments of the Minister of the Interior. The hon. member for Jacques Cartier has been able to speak of French immigration without being accused by the Minister of the Interior of raising racial prejudices, and creed questions in this House. Last year when the debate on immigration took place, to which the minister referred, my hon. friend stated that I had the honour of occupying a unique position in this House. I am sure he has found out to-night that I do not occupy a unique position in this House, and if he goes out into the country he will find that I do not occupy a unique position. Evidently the hon. gentleman has kept in his mind the debate of last year, but he has not answered the arguments made by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier to-day, or the arguments made last year by Mr. Bourassa and myself. For instance, we stated last year that although the government had cancelled its agreement with the North Atlantic Trading Company, they were still paying bonuses to booking agents ; the minister has not contradicted that. We stated last year that the policy of the North Atlantic Trading Company had been a failure, and the minister has not contradicted that to-night, nor did he last year. We stated last year that the system of paying bonuses to bring immigrants into this country had the effect of bringing people into this country of an undesirable character, and the minister has not contradicted that. We stated last year that the system of bonuses was still in existence ; the minister contradicted that last year, but he did not contradict it to-night. We stated last year that they were bringing all kinds of people to this country under the present system ; the hon. member for Jacques Cartier stated that to-night, and the minister has not dared to contradict it.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext: If I did not deny it before, I certainly take the opportunity of denying it now. But with my limited knowledge of English, I am under the impression that I did deny it.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
I am glad the hon. gentleman denies it now. I will

prove that the present immigration policy of the government is a dangerous one, and will have the result of breaking up confederation ; I will prove it by the words of the minister himself when he had no portfolio to safeguard. Take the common-sense point of view. Is there an hon. member in this House, including the minister himself, who will say that the paying of bonuses to booking agents who have nothing in common with this country, who do not know any thing about this country, has not the result of bringing to Canada a mass of immigrants without any regard to quality ? As the hon. member for Jacques Cartier stated this afternoon, there is no man in this country who would adopt the same policy for a herd of animals ; there is no man who would pay a bonus to an agent in Europe to send him a number of animals without paying any regard to their quality. But let us see what the minister said himself when he was plain Frank Oliver. In 1902 he used these words :
Let me say further that it appears to me to have been a mistake in the past to have spent so much money as we have in paying bonuses to steamship companies for the conveyance of immigrants, and for this reason:	We made
the steamship companies by that means our immigration agencies

Where is the difference this year ? If we are not making the steamship companies our immigration agents, we are making the men who sell tickets on those ships our booking agents.
-and it did not make any difference to the steamship companies what the character of the immigrant was, or where he was from so long as they got the bonus. It seems to me, from my point of view, that this is a most undesirable system and a most undesirable expense, and I would ask that it be not continued. . . . To depend on the steamship companies is to put a premium upon the worst rather than upon the better.
That is what I said a year ago, and what the hon. member for Jacques Cartier said to-night. The minister spoke thus also: I
I would like to say still further and to urge upon the House at large, upon hon. members who come from all parts of this Dominion, that the immigrant who is of the most benefit to this country in every way is the man of our own blood, namely, the native born Canadian, who, finding it necessary to shift his ground, must go either to the United States or to the Canadian Northwest.
I will prove that this government has been directing immigration from other countries, and opposing the movement from our own east to the west. But the minister, when he was still plain Frank Oliver, in 1903, said this :
Something has been said, I understand, about the paying of bounties or commissions to induce immigration. To my mind, if ever there was need for that system, that need has passed.

maintopic: SUPPLY-STATUTES OF THE PROVINCE OF SASKATCHEWAN.
speechtext:
The payment of bounties and commissions has a tendency to bring the less desirable rather than the more desirable class of people. The work of introducing immigration is carried on in many different ways. Some are better than others; and I would take the liberty of suggesting to the House that there is a certain system being carried on to day which is in every way desirable, a system which is producing the best possible results and which may very well be enlarged so as to continue these results.
But the boil, minister, before he accepted a portfolio, said that the payment of bounties had the result of bringing a less desirable class of immigrants into the country. I could go on and quote statements of the minister extending over a series of years. Even since he has been a minister he has expressed himself on this subject and notably when the North Atlantic Trading Company contract was announced. The reason given by the minister for the contract was because the government did not want to pay bounties and bonuses to individual booking agents. This is what the minister said in scoring a point against the Conservatives:
Now, to whom did our hon. friends on the other side pay the bonuses? They paid them to individual booking agents-so their letters show. To whom did this government pay in the years preceding the contract with the North Atlantic Trading Company? They paid to individual booking agents.
To whom do they pay now? Not to any individual booking agents but to the North Atlantic Trading Company, a collective interest of booking agents. And do they get value for their payments? Judged by the standard laid down in the letter of Sir Charles Tupper they do. And any man of common sense, not wrapped by political bias, will agree that that is the main question.
Since the contract has been denounced I want to ask the minister if the government pay bonuses to individual booking agents. The reason given for entering into the contract with the North Atlantic Trading Company was a false reason, or, if it were not false, how is it that the government has denounced this contract and has gone back to the system of paying bounties and bonuses to individual booking agents? The minister has been meditating on this question for twelve years and he has not given us an answer yet.
We heard this afternoon from the hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) that, with the class of people we are getting, assimilation would not be possible. The minister says that in the Northwest there is everywhere the stamp of Canadian civilization. Let us open the report of the Department of the Interior and read a list of the immigrants arriving for one month. It is as follows:
African, south; Australian, Austrian, N.E.
S.; Bohemian, Buokowinian, Croatian, Galician, Hungarian, N.E.S.; Slovak, Belgian, Bulgarian, Chinese, Dutch, French, German, N.

E.S.; Alsace-Lorraine, Prussian, English, Welsh, Scotch, Irish, West Indian, Jamaican, Greek, Hebrew, N.E.S.; Hebrew, Russian; Hebrew, Polish; Hebrew, Austrian; Hebrew, German; Italian, Japanese, Newfoundland, New Zealand, Portuguese, Poles, N.E.S.; Poles, Austrian; Poles, German; Poles Russian; Persian, Roumanian, Russian, N.E.S.; Finns, Spanish, Swiss, Servian, Danish, Icelandic, Swedish, Norwegian, Turks, Armenians, Egyptians, Syrians, Arabians, U.S.A. Citizens, India.
This is the stamp of Canadian civilization that is being put upon the Northwest. We find in a total of 109,000 immigrants, no less than 9,OuO returned Canadians. Let us go a little further. My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier pointed out this afternoon that there had been a movement started in the United States against immigration, but let us see the proportion of immigrants who come into this country and the proportion of immigrants who go to the United States. Let me point out to this House, that a man who knows something about immigration, an economist of world-wide celebrity, P. Leroy-Beaulieu, says that the immigration is greater than the natural increase of the Canadian born population. What was the population of the United States when they were receiving about the same proportion of immigrants that we are now receiving? As my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier says then they had fifty million of a population. To-day the Americans, with a population of eighty-seven million cannot assimilate one million immigrants a year; that is 115 immigrants for every 10,000 of the population. Canada, with a population of only six million received 215,000 immigrants in 1905-6. Last year we received about 300,000, or 360 to every 10,000 of the population and next year it will probably increase to 400,000 or 500,000. We have received in six years 736,000 immigrants. I see by ' Hansard ' that the unit of representation was, in 1903, 25,736. We have received enough people to supply 29 new counties in Canada. In four years at that rate we will have received enough to make 60 new counties, or 5 less than there are in Quebec, and still we are giving to the Northwest the stamp of Canadian civilization and we are assimilating this new population. The immigration which comes from the British isles has been proved to be the least desirable class in the Northwest, and this is attributable to the bonus system because it has prevented us from getting the best immigration which we could receive and that is immigration from the British isles. I am reluctant to weary the House with figures, but I desire to make a comparison between' the position of the United States and that of Canada with respect to immigration. The following table will show the proportion of immigration to population of the United States from 1790 onward:
